name: Cost allocation & transparency
desc: Who pays for the network upgrades a large load triggers, and how those costs are allocated and disclosed.

letters.desc: AEMA argues that integrating flexibility into interconnection studies defers or eliminates costly transmission upgrades, keeping costs down for all ratepayers. The FLFT creates a market-based choice: inflexible loads bear upgrade costs while flexible loads avoid them.
quotes: The FLFT would be an expedited (60-90 day) interconnection process for loads that commit to flexibility and would incorporate this flexibility into studies that determine whether transmission grid upgrades are necessary to interconnect the load.
Fast-acting load adjustments can reduce the frequency of local congestion events, defer transmission upgrades, and moderate wholesale price volatility.

AEMA believes the FLFT provides a crucial, market-based choice for large loads: (1) interconnect as an inflexible load and potentially bear the costs for the resulting, often slow and expensive, network upgrades; or (2) interconnect as a flexible load via the FLFT, avoid triggering those upgrades, and get online faster at lower cost. This protects all other ratepayers from socializing upgrade costs.

letters.desc: AEMA argues that flexible loads defer or avoid transmission upgrades, reducing costs for ratepayers. Mandating generation pairing instead would force redundant capital spending and extend supply chain backlogs, inflating the cost of AI infrastructure.
quotes: The fastest way to connect new loads that advances affordability, effectively drives investment into U.S. competitiveness and AI infrastructure rapidly, and bolsters grid reliability is to harness the full suite of flexibility technologies in a technology-neutral and performance-based way.

flexible load capabilities should be leveraged to bridge the gap between immediate interconnection needs and the longer timelines required for traditional transmission upgrades, accelerating AI infrastructure investments while also deferring or avoiding upgrades that can raise costs for ratepayers.

Mandating that every new large load be paired with new generation forces the construction of redundant capital assets when cost-effective flexibility could otherwise allow that load to be served by the existing system. This approach would unnecessarily inflate the cost of AI infrastructure and add years of supply chain backlog.

It is a fundamental principle of interconnection policy that customers who impose different impacts on the system should be treated differently. A load that is legally and technically bound to curtail during constraints does not require the same network upgrades as a static, inflexible load.

letters.desc: The filer consistently applies the principle that large loads must bear costs they cause and must not shift costs to existing ratepayers. This covers network upgrade responsibility, deposit stringency, load forecast accuracy, and limits on any crediting mechanism.
quotes: Increasing the requirements on interconnecting large load customers is critical to ensure that utilities and system operators are not planning and preparing for load that will not ultimately show up, and that load is committing to pay the cost of preparing the system. Without this discipline, other new large loads will suffer the consequences of an interconnection process bogged down by speculative projects, and all ratepayers risk being left paying the cost of preparing the system for new load that never materializes.

As with the generator interconnection process, it is critical to ensure compatibility with commercial realities and to adopt a mix of financial and non-financial readiness requirements to accommodate a range of business models and avoid a 'pay to play' model whereby well-capitalized large loads may be able to buy their way into multiple queue positions.

United agrees with what appears to be the underlying goal of these principles, which is that large loads should pay for all the services they utilize, and avoid paying for those they do not. However, United cautions that a one-size-fits-all approach is likely insufficient given the variety of possible hybrid or co-located load configurations and the range of different grid services they rely upon.

United encourages aligning cost responsibility for load interconnection with cost responsibility for generator interconnection. In that vein, it is logical that both load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades they are attributed to serve the load.
Should the Commission adopt a crediting mechanism to offset costs, this should only be applied to the extent that the network upgrades are shown to bring general benefit to load.

letters.desc: A4CRE contends that CRE utilities reduce upward pressure on transmission expansion and interconnection queues by allowing large loads to internalize their own costs and risks through private capital financing. This approach avoids cost-shifting to existing ratepayers and provides states an option for managing industrial growth without increasing consumer burden.
quotes: CRE utilities are financed entirely with private capital and do not shift costs, risks, or reliability obligations to existing ratepayers.

CRE provides a parallel, voluntary path for meeting large-load demand—particularly data centers and industrial facilities—without burdening existing systems or requiring complex interconnection studies.

CRE utilities relieve the bulk power system of the obligation to plan for and serve very large loads. By allowing those loads to internalize their own costs and risks, CRE reduces upward pressure on transmission expansion, generation additions, and interconnection queues.
For existing ratepayers, CRE reduces the likelihood of cost-shifting associated with new large loads.
CRE provides an option for managing industrial growth without compromising system reliability or increasing ratepayer exposure.

letters.desc: AES sees the existing 100% customer-pays model for network upgrades as adequate and does not support wholesale changes. It does ask for FERC guidance on how CSA termination fees and minimum-load penalties flow into transmission rates.
quotes: There is a clear role for the Commission in ensuring that certain cost-recovery mechanisms are just and reasonable (such as cost recovery related to the construction of network upgrades if a large load abandons the interconnection prior to taking retail service).

significant one-size-fits-all changes to the existing cost assignment paradigm for required network upgrades (i.e. 100% costs borne by the customer) are not needed to achieve the above considerations.

AES believes that the Commission could provide certainty to the market by issuing guidance, whether in the form of a policy statement or otherwise, regarding how termination fees from construction service agreements associated with transmission network upgrades should be accounted for in transmission rates.

letters.desc: Alliant Energy insists that hybrid facility costs for both transmission and ancillary services be allocated on a gross load basis. Netting would understate system obligations and shift costs to existing customers, conflicting with Commission precedent under Order No. 888 and the MISO OATT.
quotes: the Commission should adopt a gross load approach for both, allowing exceptions only if supported by the utility and approved by the state regulator.
Alliant Energy cautions that netting for ancillary services would understate system obligations, leading to insufficient reserves, jeopardizing reliability, and increasing costs for other customers.

letters.desc: Amazon Energy contends that stricter entry criteria, standardized milestones, and enhanced reporting will produce market efficiencies, shorter development timelines, and lower costs for consumers.
quotes: Improving the quality of large load interconnection requests through stricter criteria and milestones and enhanced visibility into the processing of large load interconnections through standardized reporting will result in market efficiencies, shorter development timelines, and lower costs for consumers.

letters.desc: Bilateral contracting and co-location with existing generation eliminate or reduce costly transmission network upgrades needed to serve new large loads.
quotes: An expedited interconnection path also would incentivize bilateral contracting between underutilized generating capacity and large loads. Such contracting would make efficient use of existing infrastructure, minimize if not eliminate the factors that have prompted premature retirement, and avoid unnecessary and costly transmission expansion.

siting new load near or at the same point of interconnection as existing generation such as a coal-fired plant can provide similar efficiencies. Therefore, the Commission should encourage interconnection studies that examine load and hybrid facilities under scenarios that consider location near existing generation to enable optimized siting, minimize network upgrade costs and delays, and enhance grid utilization.

letters.desc: ACC supports shifting upgrade costs to large load developers proportional to their actual impact, not peak demand assumptions. This protects ratepayers from subsidizing new high-demand users while incentivizing load flexibility and co-located resources.
quotes: Shifting the burden of network upgrades from ratepayers to large load project developers, largely driving current demand growth, could help alleviate near-term price surges for the broader public.
ensure that cost responsibility reflects a load's real-world impact, including any curtailment commitments or co-located generation and storage
the grid will need to at least double in capacity to maintain affordability and reliability by mid-century

letters.desc: ACORE argues that expanding high-voltage transmission and deploying grid enhancing technologies and high-performance conductors achieves cost savings and reliability benefits while meeting large load demand.
quotes: we urge the Commission to avoid focusing solely on interconnection and instead take steps to expand and modernize the transmission system to achieve the greatest cost savings and reliability benefits.
An expansion of transmission, especially long-range and high-voltage lines, is well demonstrated to achieve cost savings.
Essential to cost-effectively meeting the large load needs is an accelerated deployment of Grid Enhancing Technologies and High-Performance Conductors.

letters.desc: AEP contends that the current but-for cost assignment for generator interconnections and the lack of a clear rule for backbone transmission both block needed investment. It supports an entry fee model that gives generators upfront cost certainty, and a national postage-stamp charge for all transmission at 345 kV and above so that regional disputes do not delay grid expansion.
quotes: an approach which focuses solely on interconnecting large loads to the electric grid will not fully support rapid data center and industrial load growth.
Under this approach, all generators pay an entry fee and can rapidly connect to the grid subject to curtailment until supporting network transmission is planned and constructed.

AEP supports the widespread adoption of an entry fee model for generator interconnections, which integrates generator interconnection and transmission planning into a single streamlined process, reducing duplicative studies and expediting transmission upgrade identification.

It incorporates a predictable, transparent, and easy to calculate fee for generators to pay to connect to the grid, minimizing delays from cost disputes and preventing restudies as generators drop out of the queue due to unexpected and growing interconnection costs.
Delays and uncertainty over who must pay for transmission can prevent investment in new transmission needed to serve data centers and expanding load on the grid.
the Commission should establish a uniform national charge for all 'backbone' transmission projects—including, for example, high voltage transmission at 345 kV and above.
AEP was the first utility in the country to implement state-level tariff reforms to ensure cost recovery and preserve affordability to protect existing customers.
the Commission cannot allow parochial fights over cost allocation to slow our nation's progress and impede the connection of these loads to the system.

AEP proposes that the Commission adopt a national cost allocation for all 'backbone' transmission projects—that is, transmission lines that are extra high voltage, for example 345 kV and above (EHV transmission).

letters.desc: AEP supports rolling large load network upgrade costs into transmission rates rather than directly assigning them to interconnecting customers. This protects existing customers by making large loads pay their fair share as system users, and ensures transmission owners can attract capital for needed infrastructure.
quotes: Without much needed reforms, the current approaches threaten to produce insufficient and inefficient infrastructure to reliably support large load growth and economic development.

To protect other customers, large loads must pay their fair share for the transmission system expansion needed to serve them, and the Commission also needs to fundamentally reconsider how generator interconnection and transmission system planning are conducted to ensure that reforms drive cost-effective development to support interconnecting loads.

AEP agrees with commenters arguing that network upgrade costs for large load interconnections should be rolled into transmission rates and that direct assignment of 100% of such network upgrade costs to large load customers is not appropriate.
This is critical to ensure that transmission owners can continue to attract the capital necessary to develop the transmission infrastructure needed to support the interconnection of large loads.

While short-term speed-to-power solutions are important, the Commission cannot overlook the need to foster proactive transmission planning, which is necessary to ensure cost-effective and affordable transmission system expansion and timely interconnection of new generation resources.

letters.desc: New large loads must pay their fair share of infrastructure costs. Existing customers and wholesale transmission customers must be insulated from stranded costs if demand forecasts are not met. Network upgrade costs should be allocated to new loads. Crediting mechanisms must not harm other transmission customers.
quotes: APPA urges the Commission to consider how to implement and modify where necessary the ANOPR's principles in a way that achieves two goals: (1) continuing to allow relevant retail regulatory authorities to oversee the rates, terms, and conditions of retail service; and (2) ensuring that existing customers do not bear increased cost or increased risk as a result of Commission-jurisdictional interconnection rules for large loads.
New large loads must pay their fair share of infrastructure costs that are needed to serve them.

Wholesale transmission customers in particular could be left shouldering massive costs if new large loads do not ultimately attain or maintain the level of electricity demand that is being forecasted. The risk of stranded costs must therefore be allocated to the entities that are causing the new investment.
The ANOPR's proposal to allocate all network upgrade costs to newly interconnecting large loads would insulate existing customers from costs that would not be caused but for the new interconnection.
But such a principle should not disrupt the existing, long-standing cost allocation mechanisms that exist for planning the overall transmission system to meet the needs of load serving entities.

letters.desc: American Terawatt argues cost-of-service rate-base regulation, not capital, drives slow and oversized projects. It proposes a predetermined up-front premium for accelerated interconnection so existing ratepayers face no short-term rate increase.
quotes: The core issue is not capital. The real constraint is incentives. Utilities operate under cost-of-service regulation, where capital expenditures must be approved by regulators and then added to “rate base” to earn a regulated return.

This structure rewards utilities for undertaking larger, slower, and more capital-intensive projects, because those projects expand rate base, even when smaller or faster solutions would deliver usable grid capacity sooner.
By charging a predetermined up-front premium for this form of accelerated interconnection, utilities need not incur increased rates for consumers in the short term.

letters.org: Americans for a Clean Energy Grid
letters.desc: ACEG emphasizes that large-load interconnection requires significant regional and interregional transmission buildout at scale. Advocates for cost-allocation mechanisms that allow new costs to be shared across a larger customer base while protecting existing customers from undue burden. Positions transmission expansion as foundational, not supplementary, to interconnection success.
quotes: Interconnecting both load and generation to constrained transmission system will not be effective unless significant new grid infrastructure is built, and those new resources must be incorporated into forward-looking planning.

when managed correctly, interconnecting large loads to the grid is a win-win for all customers; the transmission system that serves everyone benefits from additional investment: new costs can be shared among a larger customer base in ways that will mitigate

We strongly support deployment of infrastructure to meet these goals, and are mindful of the need to implement the proposals in the ANOPR in a way that addresses the affordability impacts on customers and ensures harmony with state and federal jurisdiction
the grid cannot support a new era of high-density, high-demand loads without a corresponding expansion in transmission capacity.
must be understood as a core transmission-infrastructure priority one that modernizes and expands the grid at the scale required, not merely streamlines procedural steps.

new transmission infrastructure is critical to meeting large loads and enhancing the grid overall... new generation and transmission infrastructure will be part of the solution... supports expansion of the electric grid in order to enable data center growth and AI industry development

Require improved regional forecasting for significant loads (75 MW or more). Ensure cost recovery and cost-allocation mechanisms that protect existing customers while allowing large loads to participate fairly in and benefit from the broader grid. Direct proactively planned multi-value high-capacity transmission as part of the solution

the transmission system must meet the moment. No procedural refinement or queue improvement can substitute for the foundational need for more regional and interregional transmission nor for planning frameworks that anticipate, rather than react to, large-load growth.

letters.desc: Antora argues transmission charges for curtailable loads should follow cost causation and reflect actual hourly use, such as a per-MWh non-firm rate, rather than forcing flexible loads to pay as though they run around the clock. It says capacity and DNR procurement requirements yield unjust costs and that proper rates reduce NITS costs for existing ratepayers.
quotes: Antora urges the Commission, in crafting its remedy in this proceeding, to go beyond these recent reforms to require all transmission providers to: (1) offer permanent non-firm transmission service; (2) at rates reflecting actual use that is consistent with cost causation principles; (3) with curtailment requirements for non-firm load integrated into the interconnection study process and resource adequacy requirements.
An artificial DNR requirement is prohibitively expensive, unnecessary given the real-world operation of curtailable large loads like TES, and acts as a roadblock to new beneficial flexible loads.

FERC should require all jurisdictional RTOs and transmission providers to move quickly to develop and implement similar viable interconnection pathways and affordable (based on cost causation) service for large, flexible and curtailable loads.

Requiring such loads to procure generation capacity as though they consume around the clock yields unjust and unreasonable costs, contradicts cost-causation principles, and unduly discriminates against such loads by treating differently-situated customers the same.

Antora proposed an hourly utilization-based rate. This would preserve revenue from high load-factor customers while letting low load-factor loads pay only for the service they use, but this approach was not adopted for CHILLS.

Non-Firm Transmission Charges: Per-MWh billing at hourly non-firm rates (Zonal Annual Transmission Revenue Requirement/Transmission Zone Peak Load/8760) reflect the true cost causation profile of curtailable loads; directly supporting NITS costs reduction for existing ratepayers.
every jurisdictional RTO and transmission owner should be required to offer comparable, permanent, cost-causation-based non-firm service for flexible loads.

letters.desc: Arevia accepts full network upgrade cost responsibility upfront but seeks to share cost savings when hybrid operations improve system efficiency, with transmission service tied to withdrawal rights.
quotes: Arevia hybrid projects would be responsible initially for 100% of the network upgrade costs, but, if in actual system operation after the hybrid project goes commercial, the system can be shown to operate in a more efficient manner, then hybrid facilities should share in the cost savings.
If the Arevia hybrid projects are responsible 100% for NU costs, then that should allow service based on their withdrawal rights.

letters.desc: APS supports the principle that large load customers pay for costs they cause, including network and infrastructure upgrades, and seeks safeguards against cost-shifting to existing transmission or retail customer classes.
quotes: Will there be safeguards to ensure that there is no cost shift between new large load customers and other transmission or retail customer classes?

The ANOPR states that the load will be responsible for network upgrades. Will the costs be handled like network upgrades in the existing generator interconnection process, through direct assignment, or through some separate rate treatment?
Will transmission system upgrades required to deliver power to large loads qualify as network upgrade costs for the load, or just those costs required to connect them to the transmission system?
substantial infrastructure investments required to connect and serve these large loads will be paid for by those new large load customers, not existing customers.

letters.desc: The filer argues that dispatchable generation and hybrid resources deliver resource adequacy more economically than curtailment-only models. Verifiable dispatchable loads combined with generation increase system output cost-effectively while maintaining reliability and benefiting the rate base.
quotes: for hybrid sites constituting a mix of generation and load resources behind a point of interconnection, the total range of dispatchable capacity should be a measurable and performance-based commodity that can be procured, scheduled, compensated, and held to emergency operating conditions much like traditional generating capacity.

When the proposed load itself is verifiably dispatchable, system reliability is maintained. When new load is combined with net new generation capacity and/or dispatchable resources that increase the total energy output of the system, resource adequacy is achieved more economically, to the benefit of the rate base.

in the course of normal grid operations, it is far less expensive and far more reliable to meet incremental resource adequacy needs with supplemental generation, whether located on-site or electrical proximal, than to compensate a large load for curtailing

letters.desc: Buckeye argues that data centers drive massive transmission investments that, if the load fails to materialize or sustain, will be stranded on uninvolved wholesale customers. Buckeye supports ANOPR Principle 8 requiring large loads to pay 100% of network upgrade costs upfront, with a crediting mechanism only if designed to protect other customers. Fallback options -- holding the host utility responsible or requiring retail protections to flow into wholesale rates -- are also supported.
quotes: There is serious concern that these large loads could drive significant transmission investment and then not show up to pay for it on a sustained basis.

If a large load fails to materialize or consume electricity at the level and duration expected when these transmission investments were made, other wholesale transmission customers (and, ultimately, their retail customers) may be faced with the massive costs of investments they did not cause.

Because the Commission is obligated under the Federal Power Act ("FPA") to ensure that rates under its jurisdiction are just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory, the Commission must ensure that large loads are responsible for the cost of transmission facilities built to serve them so other wholesale customers are not left holding the bag.

Buckeye supports holding large loads such as data centers directly responsible for 100% of the network upgrades they are assigned through interconnection studies (which could include crediting, provided that crediting is designed to ensure that wholesale transmission customers are protected).

Although these requirements may prevent speculative projects from entering the study process, they do not address the major stranded cost concerns with data centers that complete the study process, cause massive transmission upgrades, but then do not have the expected level of demand over a sustained period.
Load growth of approximately 10,000 MW driven largely by data centers in the Dominion Zone of PJM resulted in approximately $12 billion in transmission investment across PJM.
While these costs are primarily driven by data center loads, currently all customers in the corresponding PJM transmission zones and, where applicable, in the broader PJM region will bear them.

If the relevant wholesale transmission entity, like AEP Ohio, were responsible for the network upgrade costs caused by their retail customers seeking large load interconnections, that could both protect other wholesale transmission customers and still allow a mechanism for ultimately holding large loads responsible for the costs they cause.

At a minimum (and as a transition mechanism before upfront funding measures take effect, as discussed in Part III.D below), the Commission must ensure that any existing retail-level protections against the risks of stranded costs of Commission-jurisdictional transmission service resulting from large loads will be reflected and accounted for in Commission-jurisdictional rates.
Under AEP Ohio's retail tariff, these measures protect only AEP Ohio's own retail customers from these significant stranded transmission cost risks, leaving wholesale transmission customers exposed.
It is absolutely essential that this Commission address these issues and cost shifting concerns at the federal level.
An appropriate crediting mechanism for this purpose will need to be different from the crediting mechanism used for large generator interconnections.

letters.desc: Buckeye consistently invokes cost causation and beneficiary-pays principles to support direct assignment of transmission upgrade costs to data centers. Buckeye opposes rolled-in pricing, nationalized postage stamp rates, and any mechanism that socializes data center costs to other wholesale customers.
quotes: Large loads, particularly data centers, are driving historic investments in the transmission grid, which have the very real risk of creating significant cost shifts if the large loads do not show up to pay for this investment on a sustained basis.

A wholesale solution is necessary to ensure that the significant impacts to Commission-jurisdictional transmission rates that data centers are causing do not result in significant cost shifts to other wholesale transmission customers, like Buckeye.

Direct assignment of upfront costs is the only approach that ensures other ratepayers are not left holding the bag if a large load does not show up on a sustained basis to pay for the investments it has caused.

Rolled-in approaches would force other customers to bear costs they did not cause and expose them to significant stranded cost risk. That is particularly inappropriate given the unique scale, pace, and cost shift risks associated with large data center interconnections.
Buckeye opposes American Electric Power Service Corporation's ("AEP's") proposal to socialize data center transmission costs to other customers on a nationwide basis.
"and" pricing concerns should not deter the Commission from requiring upfront funding by data centers of the transmission additions they cause.

Crediting would provide the large data center with the opportunity to receive full credits for its upfront payments to the extent that it has sufficient usage over a sustained period of time, thereby protecting other wholesale customers from bearing stranded costs.

Under this approach, the relevant wholesale transmission entity (not the data center end-user itself) would be held responsible for data center-caused costs at the wholesale level, and that entity could then pass through these costs to the data centers as they and retail regulators see fit at the retail level.
Retail-only solutions are insufficient. Buckeye opposes retail-only solutions that fail to address transmission cost shifting to other wholesale customers.

if the Commission does not adopt a wholesale framework consistent with Principle 8 (as described above in Parts II.A and II.B), it must at minimum ensure that retail-level protections against stranded data center transmission costs are reflected at the wholesale level to ensure just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory Commission-jurisdictional rates.
The Commission cannot assume that agreements negotiated between one utility and a data center will be sufficiently protective of other customers.
The approach of reflecting retail-level solutions in Commission-jurisdictional rates (Part II.C.ii above) should be applied to any large data centers already being studied for interconnection.

letters.desc: The central concern throughout the filing is that other wholesale transmission customers, including Buckeye, face billions in stranded costs from data center-driven network upgrades if FERC does not act. Buckeye criticizes the AEP Ohio retail tariff and similar state measures as protecting only retail customers of the serving utility, not other wholesale customers. It also warns that bilateral agreements and the Mobile-Sierra presumption are inadequate substitutes for a clear FERC rule.
quotes: Contrary to NARUC's assertions, state action alone cannot protect all customers against transmission cost shifting caused by data centers. Federal action is necessary to protect all customers against transmission cost shifting.
Without action by the Commission, wholesale transmission customers like Buckeye, and the retail customers of its members, could be left shouldering billions in transmission costs.
To best protect other customers, the Commission should require large loads to be responsible for 100% of the network upgrade costs they cause.

Retail regulators can address the relationship between the data center, the utility serving that data center at retail, and that utility's other retail customers. But they lack authority to address the impact on other customers affected by data center-driven transmission costs.

Although the Ohio Commission explicitly acknowledged concerns about cost shifts to other wholesale transmission customers, it declined to take any action to address them. Instead, it found that these issues 'are statutorily outside of [the PUCO's] intrastate purview.'

Buckeye supports the ANOPR's proposal to hold large loads 100% responsible for the network upgrade costs they cause, which is the most protective and direct way to ensure that other customers are protected against the unique and significant risks posed by these large loads.

FERC could hold the relevant wholesale transmission entity with the direct relationship to the large load responsible for large load-driven network upgrade costs, as that entity would be in a position to pass these costs onto the large load under its retail arrangements.
Allowing utilities to address data center stranded cost issues through bilateral agreements or retail tariffs is problematic and an inferior solution compared to those discussed above in Part II.B.

Unlike in the context of bilateral agreements to which the Mobile-Sierra presumption is typically applied, there is no reason to assume that an agreement negotiated between one utility and a data center will sufficiently protect other customers from the agreement's significant impact on transmission rates.
Data centers have likely caused over $24 billion in RTEP projects so far.

FERC must act and provide a clear directive to TOs and RTOs to protect the other wholesale customers and their retail customers against transmission cost shifting, whether this be through a rule, show cause order, policy statement, or other Commission action.

letters.desc: RTO cost allocation must reflect cost-causation principles and be based on customers' actual contributions to peak periods and system drivers, not maximum withdrawal rights. Clear pricing signals tied to constraint periods incentivize grid-positive behavior and reduce the need for additional infrastructure.
quotes: Maintain clear, fair RTO-level cost allocation mechanisms that reflect customers' contributions to the drivers of new infrastructure. While states will maintain jurisdiction over retail rates, RTOs can allocate costs to Load Serving Entities in a manner that better aligns cost causation and cost allocation. The grid will be more affordable if price signals encourage behavior that reduces the need for additional infrastructure.

The Commission should ensure that cost allocation to large load customers for transmission service associated with infrastructure not assigned through the interconnection study process is being allocated to those large load customers in a manner that appropriately reflects cost-causation principles. If new large loads are taking transmission service through a FERC jurisdictional interconnection process, then this process should cover all aspects of transmission service.

Transmission service should be assessed based on cost-causation principles and not based on maximum withdrawal rights. Transmission service is typically assessed upon customers' contribution to coincident peak demand. The transmission owners and RTO/ISOs should determine which periods or system conditions drive the need for system investment and assess costs based on those periods of time. This creates clear pricing signals to incentivize behavior which will reduce the need for additional investment.

letters.org: California Department of Water Resources State Water Project
letters.desc: DWR supports holding new large loads financially responsible for 100% of triggered network upgrade costs and designing a crediting mechanism that keeps existing wholesale customers whole, preventing speculative interconnection requests from shifting costs onto ratepayers.
quotes: New large interconnections should finance 100% of the network upgrades they are assigned through the interconnection study process.
If massive transmission investments are made to serve these loads, yet the expected demand does not materialize, other customers may be left holding the bag.

This assignment of costs should be paired with an appropriate crediting mechanism. This crediting mechanism might vary from region-to-region, but it must be designed to keep wholesale customers whole and disincentivize speculative load that will impose costs on wholesale customers.
Such a guaranteed crediting mechanism should not be adopted for large load interconnections because these credits are not tied to particular levels of usage.

letters.desc: CAISO supports assigning network upgrade costs to large load customers and endorses net-rights-based upgrade sizing for hybrids with proper protection facilities. CAISO asks for a clear rule on which cost responsibility regime applies to hybrid facilities.
quotes: Hybrid facilities that have strict, unwavering protections like circuit breakers at their point of interconnection should be allowed to have network upgrades based on their net rights requested.  This will save ratepayers and developers from unnecessary costs and help to avoid long construction timelines.

the CAISO requests that any final rule provide clear guidance on cost responsibility for hybrid facilities: Separating which network upgrades were required by a generator and which network upgrades were required by a co-located large load is impractical, if at all possible for some types of upgrades.

letters.desc: The CPUC supports public posting of cost responsibility determinations, annual consumer cost impact reports, and transparent methodology for cost causation. Costs from large load transmission upgrades should not be shifted to other ratepayers without clear, standardized criteria.
quotes: FERC has consistently recognized, including in Order Nos. 2003 and 2023, that interconnection service is distinct from transmission service.  Yet under the ANOPR's reasoning, the act of connecting a large retail customer directly to transmission facilities could transform that retail delivery into a FERC-jurisdictional wholesale transaction – redefining distribution facilities and costs as transmission assets, shifting oversight of distribution expansion, maintenance, and rate recovery from state commissions to FERC.

either this process would slow energization of large load and extend the timeline for bringing AI data centers online, or these questions would go unaddressed, resulting in unreasonable cost-shifting and a less reliable electric grid for all.
transparency measures "are necessary to protect residential consumers from bearing the costs of overbuilt transmission infrastructure resulting from inaccurate or inflated demand projections."

the Commission should require public utilities, Regional Transmission Organizations and Independent System Operators to provide public posting of:  1. All interconnection requests above [the MW threshold], including project type and location;  2. Cost responsibility determinations and any resulting upgrades; and   3. Annual reporting on the consumer cost impacts of large-load interconnections, associated transmission expansions, and the impact on electricity and capacity markets rates for consumers other than large loads.

Transparency in methodology for cost causation and cost allocation is critical to ensure the costs related to large load customers transmission network upgrades ("TNU's") are not unreasonably allocated in electricity rates to other customers.

letters.desc: The filing contends that CRE utilities, funded entirely by private capital, prevent cost shifts to existing ratepayers and reduce strain on regulated utilities. It frames CRE as a cost-free alternative to public financing of new large-load infrastructure.
quotes: CRE utilities would offer economic and reliability benefits to the broader community by reducing the strain on regulated utilities and protecting existing ratepayers from the financial risks of overspending on infrastructure upgrades.

Consumer Regulated Electricity (CRE) is a permissionless model that allows new, privately financed, islanded electric utilities to serve new industrial and datacenter loads without relying on taxpayer funds, existing ratepayers, congested transmission systems, or fragile grids.
CRE offers a parallel path—privately built capacity that adds supply without affecting regulated rates or queues.

letters.desc: The Center supports strict enforcement of ANOPR Principle 8, requiring large-load customers to cover 100% of network upgrade costs and protecting ratepayers from stranded-asset exposure. Utilities currently shift data center costs through special contracts, mismatched federal-state cost allocation, and co-location loopholes.
quotes: the Commission should adopt clear rules preventing any cost-shifting of network upgrades or stranded assets attributable to large-load customers.

Because data centers both cause and benefit from these upgrades, the Commission must rigorously enforce Principle 8. This includes conducting transparent load interconnection studies and requiring large-load customers to cover 100% of their network upgrade costs, while also strengthening the principle to ensure ratepayers are protected from any stranded-asset costs.

utilities are getting away with socializing the costs of the data center boom, and simultaneously keeping rates low to attract data centers, by: (1) entering into special contracts; (2) taking advantage of discrepancies between federal and state regulations over cost allocation; and (3) relying on co-location agreements.

PJM spent $5.1 billion on new transmission, and half of those costs were distributed to member utilities based on their share of power demand... in Maryland for example, residential ratepayers will then pay for two-thirds of the state's overall share in transmission costs, even though PJM is building this new transmission for Virginia data centers and not the average Maryland residential ratepayer.

letters.org: CHAMBER OF COMMERCE OF THE UNITED STATES
letters.desc: Cost allocation should be fair, transparent, and tied to a clear methodology. Large loads should pay their full cost of service so that interconnections lower rather than raise rates for other customers, with costs assigned in proportion to benefits from upgrades.
quotes: Cost Allocation Transparency: It is essential that the costs associated with interconnecting large loads are allocated in a fair and transparent manner. Clear cost allocation methodologies will provide certainty to large load customers and generation and transmission developers and ensure that costs are equitably allocated, as appropriate, across relevant stakeholder constituencies.

large loads are committed to paying their full cost of service for the energy and infrastructure supporting the electric service they require. Ultimately, large load interconnections should result in lower, rather than elevated, electricity rates for all other customers. The Commission's efforts to streamline large load interconnections should ensure that costs are allocated commensurate with the benefits received from any needed network upgrades.

letters.desc: Chevron supports developing a rulemaking that accords with the DOE ANOPR's fourteen principles, which include cost allocation and upgrade cost considerations for large load interconnections.
quotes: The Commission should move forward with a rulemaking that generally accords with, and further develops, the fourteen principles set forth in the DOE ANOPR.

letters.desc: CEBA supports a cost-causation framework where large loads pay for upgrades they trigger but share in broader benefits. Rates must reflect actual usage at specific locations, not broad averages, and studies should be based on realistic operating behavior to avoid unnecessary upgrade costs.
quotes: A cost-allocation framework grounded in cost causation is essential to preventing unjust and unreasonable outcomes. Large loads should pay for upgrades required for their interconnection, but should similarly receive the broader benefits that those upgrades may provide to other grid customers.

Any cost allocation rules that emerge from this proceeding should avoid setting load interconnection rates using overly generalized estimates or broad averages that bear little or no relationship to anticipated usage at specific locations on the transmission system.

FERC should also require transmission providers to study large-load interconnection requests based on realistic operating behavior, like the approach in Order 2023 for storage resources, to improve accuracy, avoid unnecessary upgrades, and reduce excessive costs.

letters.desc: ClearPath recommends that FERC set guardrails preventing cost-shifting and free riding without prescribing a single methodology, so that utilities can experiment with rate designs. It favors combining volumetric and coincident peak demand charges to incentivize load shifting and cites a critical peak pricing pilot where electric arc furnaces reduced peak loads by 91%.
quotes: developers of both generation and large loads often submit multiple interconnection requests as a means of price discovery and time-to-grid discovery. This creates unmanageable queue volumes, inflated demand and supply forecasts, and significant delays to the interconnection process due to projects withdrawing late into the process when they discover their project is not economically feasible due to costs or energization timelines.

Coordinating interconnection studies for large loads with supply-side interconnection can enable the identification of more cost-effective transmission solutions and ensure that all benefiting customers pay, whether they are load or supply customers.

We recommend that FERC adopt a similar approach for studying large load withdrawals and/or injections. This advances just and reasonable rates by avoiding overestimation of the impacts of large loads through study assumptions that depict worst-case scenarios, such as curtailable large loads withdrawing at full capacity during peak demand periods

ClearPath recommends that FERC establish clear guardrails for how utilities serving large loads allocate costs for transmission and ancillary services to prevent cost-shifting or free riding, rather than prescribing a particular methodology.

Cost-allocation of network upgrades that combine volumetric and coincident peak demand charges can incentivize flexible large loads to avoid system peaks, therefore reducing system impacts and the need for additional infrastructure investments.
This regulatory framework incentivized EAFs to curtail load during critical peak demand and shift production, leading to a reduction of peak loads by 91%.

letters.desc: AI-SCA accepts that interconnecting large load customers should remain responsible for the costs of associated network upgrades. It sees alternative supply arrangements like co-location and behind-the-meter generation as ways to manage those costs while accelerating connection.
quotes: Meeting the growing demand from new, critical large loads requires accelerating interconnection processes and establishing additional pathways for large loads to connect to the transmission system in ways that manage costs and preserve long-term reliability for all customers.

Approaches such as direct market access and new supply arrangements, such as co-location (or hybrid facilities), bring your own power, and behind-the-meter generation, can enable faster connection to the grid for large load customers like data centers, reshoring of manufacturing, and other industrial processes while ensuring that interconnecting customers are responsible for associated costs of network upgrades.

letters.desc: Committee strongly supports requiring large data center loads to fully bear all interconnection and network upgrade costs, with transparency mechanisms and financial commitments including deposits and take-or-pay contracts. Opposes cost crediting mechanisms that would offset these expenses.
quotes: We write to urge you to prioritize holding American families harmless from the costs imposed upon the nation's grid by large loads, including data centers, as you consider the advanced notice of proposed rulemaking (ANOPR) submitted to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) by the Department of Energy (DOE).

The affordability of electricity in America is under threat. Residential retail electricity prices have risen 13 percent since the start of the year, tripling the rate of general inflation. And power demand from data centers is set to increase dramatically, potentially further jeopardizing consumer bills.

Data centers could represent anywhere between 7 to 12 percent of American electricity demand by 2028, and one aggregate of utility forecasts showed an expected increase in peak demand of 120 gigawatts (GW) by 2029, or nearly 15 percent.
Studies have indicated that residential power bills are already subsidizing data center buildouts.
They cannot be built out on the backs of the power bills of American families across the country.

FERC should aim to ensure that grid facilities and upgrades are only developed for loads that are certain to be built and ensure that those large load customers fully bear the cost of their interconnection facilities and network upgrades.
FERC should also demand transparency mechanisms so it and other appropriate regulators can verify that these conditions are being met.

We strongly support introducing a parallel version of some of these reforms, such as establishing a 'first-ready, first served' process, imposing large study deposits, increasing financial commitments from load interconnection customers, and increasing financial penalties for withdrawn requests.

Given the significant impacts that large data center loads can have on local grids, FERC should consider requiring large loads to sign take-or-pay commitments with transmission providers, with the largest customers being subject to the most stringent requirements.

Large load facilities should be responsible for all of the network upgrades assigned to them through the interconnection study process, but do not support offsetting those costs via a crediting mechanism.
FERC should require sufficient transparency from grid operators so it can determine which specific large load facilities are responsible for specific grid upgrade needs.

letters.desc: Constellation supports transmission rates that reflect the actual quantity of capacity and energy flowing to a large load over the grid, varying by service type (firm, generator-contingent, interruptible). It opposes a one-size-fits-all gross NITS charge and argues net billing is consistent with how PJM already handles behind-the-meter generation.
quotes: the Commission should allow the transmission services customers want and rates that reflect the quantity of capacity and energy being transmitted to them over the grid.

Charging all large loads a "NITS rate [network transmission rate] based on gross load (as opposed to net) no matter their actual use of the transmission system discriminates because such a construct 'is incapable of differentiating customers who impose different costs on the transmission system through co-location.'

Replacing PJM's Necessary Study process with RMR/SSR retirement studies that would impose broad new network costs on a class of existing resources for the simple act of serving a customer through a co-located configuration chosen by the customer, which may be the only option to serve the load in a timely fashion.
It is highly discriminatory to charge these costs to resources entering into such arrangements compared to resources that are actually retiring altogether which are not burdened with these costs.

the Commission should also immediately issue an order in the PJM Show Cause proceedings ... adopting the Commission's preliminary finding that the PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable and establishing a replacement rate based on the record in those proceedings that reflects the ANOPR's guidance

letters.desc: Constellation argues that gross billing for hybrid facilities is unfair since co-located generation reduces actual grid use, and supports netting transmission charges. It also opposes rate-basing upgrade costs and calls for market-based reliability backstop mechanisms rather than discriminatory BYOG conditions.
quotes: Discrimination against existing generation resources will undermine resource adequacy by signaling that existing capacity is less valuable than new capacity in serving load, even when existing capacity can serve load more efficiently.

The Commission should let existing market mechanisms work to ensure resource adequacy. If it determines that reform is needed, it should adopt competitive market fixes that preserve market-based incentives for capital investment, such as the Joint Stakeholders' Reliability Backstop Alternative

Constellation agrees with netting charges for hybrid facilities "as that value amount reflects the quantity of capacity and energy that is being transmitted across the transmission system to the load." ... it is not "fair" to ignore the fact that a hybrid facility load is being directly served by a generator and thus not relying on "capacity and energy … being transmitted across the transmission system" in assessing charges.

Rolling billions of dollars of network upgrades into rate base is not an intuitive way of "protecting customers." Regardless, the Commission's policy should create strong incentives for co-location because co-location minimizes upgrade costs, and that is ultimately what protects consumers.

letters.desc: Constellation argues LCEP achieves speed-to-service without imposing new costs on other customers because it uses existing studied infrastructure rather than triggering new network upgrades.
quotes: LCEP Service is one of the simplest and most efficient ways to achieve speed-to-service without jeopardizing reliability or increasing costs to other customers.

letters.desc: Large loads and hybrid facilities should bear 100 percent of upgrade costs assigned in interconnection studies. This aligns with cost causation principles in utility ratemaking, prevents cross-subsidy, and protects system reliability by ensuring costs fall on those who cause them.
quotes: load and hybrid facilities should be Responsible for 100% of the upgrades that they are assigned through interconnection studies.
This sentiment aligns with the cost causation principle of utility ratemaking which limits cross subsidies and protects system reliability by requiring that costs be borne by those who cause them.

letters.desc: The filer argues that when enforceable LLFC controls materially bound a site's withdrawal risk, base upgrade requirements should reflect the LLFC envelope rather than the non-performance sensitivity. This would lower interconnection costs for flexible loads.
quotes: base upgrade requirements should not be set by those sensitivities when enforceable LLFC controls materially bound risk

letters.desc: Critical Loop agrees that large loads should pay the marginal costs they cause, but argues that LLFC customers effectively internalize much of their interconnection cost. High-load-factor customers can also spread fixed costs across more energy sales, putting downward pressure on average rates. Cost causation principles should recognize both sides: loads pay what they cause and receive expedited treatment when they demonstrably reduce system costs.
quotes: An LLFC-style flexible connection can address the transmission bottleneck by defining a mix of firm and conditional service within an operating envelope, while complementary "bring your own capacity" mechanisms can address the generation bottleneck by ensuring that the firm portion of the load is backed by accredited capacity paid for by the customer.
when a large load accepts a flexible connection and procures or brings capacity sufficient to meet its firm service, it is effectively internalizing much of the marginal cost of its interconnection.

because large loads often operate at higher load factors than the system average, these customers can improve utilization of existing transmission and generation assets. Fixed costs are then recovered over a larger volume of energy sales, which can put downward pressure on average rates over time.

Large loads should pay the costs they cause, and they should receive appropriate treatment, including access to expedited, flexible interconnection pathways and transparent queue treatment, when they verifiably reduce needed system investments and help lower long-run costs for other ratepayers through LLFC-style commitments and bring-your-own-capacity arrangements.

letters.desc: Transmission and ancillary service charges should be calculated on the net power actually withdrawn from the grid, not on total facility consumption. Crusoe cites ERCOT's generation-netting settlement as a model.
quotes: Large loads and hybrid facilities should thus pay their fair share of current and future grid costs based on their use of the grid.

letters.desc: Advanced conductors substantially reduce interconnection costs compared to new transmission construction. CTC highlights the Southern California Edison case, where reconductoring with advanced conductors reduced project costs from 135 million to 48 million dollars (65 percent savings) while increasing capacity by 60 percent in 18 months.
quotes: Reconductoring with advanced conductors is a proven, fast, and cost-effective way to create transmission headroom on existing corridors.

Carbon composite core advanced conductors can double the capacity on existing structures because they do not have the increase in weight and sag necessary when capacity is increased with early and mid-1900s steel core conductors like ACSR and ACSS.

Southern California Edison reconductored 137 miles of its 230 kV Big Creek transmission corridor with ACCC Conductor, avoiding a costly rebuild while eliminating sag violations and adding more than 60% additional line capacity. The project cut costs from $135 million to $48 million, reduced completion time from 48 to 18 months, improved safety, lowered line losses by 30%, and delivered significant environmental and customer savings.
Reconductoring with advanced conductors costs far less than building new lines—savings that translate into lower electricity bills for American families and reduced energy costs for businesses.

letters.desc: DPN seeks crediting of network upgrade costs over the PPA and an option for the interconnection customer to build, preventing a transmission-owner construction monopoly that could delay projects or raise costs.
quotes: the upgrade costs need to be credited back to the facility over the course the power purchase agreement (PPA) length. The maximum duration for issuing the credit should be 50% of the PPA length.
This prevents the transmission owner from having a monopoly on construction that could delay projects or raise costs.

letters.desc: EDF supports the beneficiary pays principle applied to hybrid loads: flexible, grid-light loads should pay lower charges than firm loads, sleeve transaction costs should be eliminated through PUHCA reform, and network load charges should fall only on loads that materially rely on the grid.
quotes: regulatory limitations on EWGs prevent IPPs from making direct sales to hybrid facility load even if the relevant state jurisdiction would allow such direct sales.  This can be a significant impediment to data center development, causing unnecessary delay and increased costs.

The sleeve requirement for the generation component of a hybrid facility is an inefficient transaction structure and increases costs – by unnecessarily imposing an REP "middleman" requirement in every transaction.

It is appropriate for large loads and hybrid facilities to pay for network upgrades required for their interconnection and transmission service based on their rights-based interconnection obligations.  As noted above, hybrid facilities should be able to benefit from reduced network upgrade costs by studying co-located generation and load together.

Hybrid structures that are dispatchable and/or curtailable and place minimum demands on the transmission system (i.e., "grid-light") should pay less in grid costs than co-location structures where the load requires five-nines reliability.  Services provided by curtailable load should be eligible for demand response revenues.  This is required by the Commission's beneficiary pays principle.
Only co-location structures with load that regularly and materially use the grid should pay network load transmission charges, consistent with the Commission's beneficiary pays principle.

letters.desc: EEI supports a cost allocation framework that spreads network upgrade costs through rolled-in rates while using financial commitments from large load customers to protect other ratepayers if a project does not materialize.
quotes: Rather than only directly assigning costs of the network upgrades necessary to connect large load customers, the Commission should require them to pay for their share of the transmission system.

The Commission's longstanding precedent is that network upgrade costs are rolled into transmission providers' rates and charged to all system customers. As a result, all customers pay for their share of the transmission system based on their connection to and use of the system and thus, large load customers will, by virtue of their size, pay for their proportional share of the costs.

letters.desc: EEI favors allocating transmission and ancillary service costs to large loads on a gross-load basis, treating them as users of the integrated system rather than carved-out customers. EEI argues this is the most consumer-protective approach and that network upgrades for large loads benefit all grid users, making direct assignment inappropriate.
quotes: Any cost allocation policy adopted in this proceeding should do two things: (1) ensure large load customers pay for the costs that they impose on the transmission system, and (2) protect everyday Americans from adverse impacts and costs from interconnecting new large loads.

large loads should not receive special carved-out treatment (namely, by only paying directly assigned costs for network upgrades), but rather they should be responsible for paying their fair share of the relevant transmission system, including both network upgrades they caused and the existing system they benefit from, like all other users.

network upgrades are "integrated with and support the ... overall Transmission System for the general benefit of all users of such Transmission System."  By their very definition, they benefit the entire system, akin to a widened highway connecting busy commercial regions.

Adopting a default rule that allocates the costs of transmission service for co-located or hybrid large loads based on net injection/withdrawal rights will create adverse cost impacts for other customers and is not necessary to achieve the goals of the DOE ANOPR.

the entire arrangement is connected to and reliant on the broader system.  As one example, there is a possibility that the generation component of a hybrid facility becomes unavailable, and the full load (i.e., without netting) looks to non-co-located resources to be served.
EEI's recommended approach--a default cost-allocation rule based on gross load for both transmission service and ancillary services--is the measured, most consumer-protective approach.

letters.desc: EEI consistently emphasizes that large load customers must pay their fair share and that state tariffs with minimum billing demands, exit fees, and financial assurance requirements protect other ratepayers. The filing treats existing state-level cost protections as sufficient.
quotes: EEI member companies are committed to working collaboratively with states, large load customers, the Commission, and other stakeholders to ensure the timely interconnection of large loads while protecting all customers and the grid.

EEI emphasized that members have been working with their state regulators, customers, and other stakeholders to integrate large loads into the electric system through state-regulated large load tariffs and bilateral retail service agreements.
Twenty states have approved at least one large load tariff, and another 9 states have pending large load tariffs.

State commissions across the country have approved or are considering large load tariffs, processes, service regulations, and contractual terms, which are all tools in a broader strategy that electric companies and states can implement to reduce risk and protect customers.
Large load tariffs, processes, service regulations, and contractual terms are all tools in a broader strategy that electric companies and states can implement to reduce risk and protect customers.

letters.desc: EPSA strongly opposes proposals that would allow transmission owners to build and rate-base new generation, arguing this would raise consumer costs, shift risk to ratepayers, and reverse two decades of competitive market policy. Any reform should rest on market-based mechanisms rather than reregulation.
quotes: this proceeding is being utilized as an opportunity to press unwarranted attacks on our nation's competitive power markets in an attempt to hijack this critical emergent concern to dismantle competitive mechanisms and allow monopolistic behavior to flourish further.
Fundamentally, monopoly ownership stifles competition, increases consumer costs, distorts markets, and unfairly shifts financial risk from investors to ratepayers.

Allowing transmission owners to return to the business of building and operating rate-based generation after Order No. 2000 was established to resolve massive cost overruns and poor operating performance under the previous regime should not be part of any solution.
In this uncertain environment, competitive markets place the risk of investment to meet load growth on shareholders rather than ratepayers.

A reliance on innovative market-based mechanisms should be the foundation of any next step in this rulemaking proceeding, while plaintive calls to reregulate should be dismissed for what they are – self-serving mis-directions which will not help us achieve our national goals.

letters.desc: ELCON strongly endorses cost causation so large loads bear upgrade costs rather than spreading them to other customers. It also asks for flexibility in financial mechanisms and self-build options, and raises concern that well-capitalized developers could displace industrial applicants in the queue if readiness obligations are set too high.
quotes: We caution the Commission to be aware that developers with massive amounts of capital can push other projects, that struggle to meet steep readiness obligations, further down the interconnection queue.
ELCON agrees with principle eight that load be responsible for any necessary network upgrades necessary to connect their facilities to the grid.

We ask that the Commission provide flexibility in the financial and crediting mechanisms to pay for those upgrade costs as well as provide the option to build those upgrades as set out in principle nine.

the Commission should expand upon Principle 12 to actively encourage large loads to become system solutions. Curtailable and dispatchable large loads provide a demonstrable system benefit akin to essential ancillary services (such as operating and contingency reserves). The final rule must establish clear mechanisms to compensate these customers for the reliability value they provide, creating a critical financial incentive to offer flexible service that ultimately defers costly transmission and generation build-out for the benefit of all ratepayers.

letters.desc: ECA supports requiring large loads to pay 100% of assigned upgrade costs and favors cost causation principles broadly. The filing also calls for mandatory transparency on how interconnection costs flow into retail rates so states and customers can contest them.
quotes: leveraging opportunities for these quickly emerging large loads to utilize flexible arrangements to secure and pay for their own power supply—such as the hybrid (sometimes called "co-location") arrangements described by the Secretary in the ANOPR, "bring your own power" models, utilization of behind the meter generation and microgrids, and the like—is also essential to addressing threats to customer affordability and ensuring that private investors, not captive ratepayers, take on the costs and risks of rapid large load growth.

the Commission should require transmission providers to provide additional transparency of how costs incurred to interconnect to the FERC-jurisdictional transmission system will flow through to state retail tariffs.

ECA supports measures that ensure that all customers pay for the costs they cause and for the benefits they receive. A guideline requiring load and hybrid facilities to pay for 100% of the network upgrades they are assigned is sensible on its face and consistent with how generators are treated.

letters.desc: ECA emphasizes that other customers face cost shift and stranded cost risk from large load growth, and calls for transparency in how interconnection costs are incurred and allocated. ECA opposes mandates that restrict private capital options, arguing they raise costs without benefit to existing customers.
quotes: Other customers lack sufficient transparency into how costs are incurred and allocated and in forecasts of new large loads to have confidence that investments made to serve new large loads are not being shifted to them or exposing them to stranded cost risk.

The Commission should, as a general matter, avoid taking options off the table for large customers to fund with private capital rather than ratepayer funds the new transmission and generation infrastructure needed to serve them.

Mandating that all transmission upgrades be funded by transmission providers in rate base with a return on investment, or that customers securitize network upgrades that transmission providers are funding through rate base, would lead to increased costs and less options to support speed to power without any demonstrable benefit to other customers.

letters.desc: Emerald AI argues the near-zero marginal cost of software flexibility makes it far cheaper than new transmission, and that the existing tariff structure forces ratepayers to subsidize upgrades that could be avoided. The filing supports directing upgrade costs to loads that remain inflexible and exempting those that deliver verified flexibility.
quotes: The greatest opportunity in this rulemaking is not merely streamlining the administrative study process, but enabling large loads to actively avoid or defer massive grid and energy infrastructure upgrades.
the marginal cost of software-based flexibility is near-zero (operating expense), whereas the marginal cost of new transmission capacity is extremely high (capital expense).

Transmission service frameworks do not yet exist to allow for load flexibility to avoid network upgrades. Network Integration Transmission Service at the wholesale level is non-interruptible under FERC's pro forma tariff. And, while non-firm point-to-point service does exist, there is no non-firm network option for a load to access and draw upon the full network during times it is not curtailed. Nor do utilities studying large load interconnection generally provide a pathway through which a curtailable customer can be studied to avoid network upgrades.

projects that remain inflexible proceed through the standard process and may bear upgrade-related costs, whereas projects that commit to and deliver flexibility can avoid or reduce those upgrades and connect sooner.

letters.desc: LCDG ensures that new large loads invest in needed generation resources at interconnection, preventing stranded costs from falling on existing ratepayers.
quotes: LCDG would mitigate the risk of stranded infrastructure costs falling upon existing grid customers because it would ensure that new large loads would be investing in needed generation resources as they interconnect to the transmission system.

letters.desc: Enchanted Rock ties co-location to ratepayer protection, arguing that studying co-located assets together triggers fewer transmission upgrades and mitigates costs that would otherwise be passed onto ratepayers.
quotes: This observation highlights the value of co-location and its practical application to facilitate speed-to-power, expedite study timelines, protect ratepayer affordability, and reduce strain on transmission infrastructure.
Co-locating generation with load allows system planners to

letters.desc: ETI contends that uplift payments, opaque demand response, and congestion derivative underfunding each distort prices and raise costs to consumers and investors. The filing asks FERC and DOE to eliminate these distortions through market-based reforms rather than administrative interventions.
quotes: Without proper price formation, market participants and investors are left "groping about in the dark" as to what types of interconnection projects would be useful and profitable, regardless of whether and how the jurisdictional considerations are ultimately resolved.

price suppressing events remain a persistent problem in these markets––even as recently as with the PJM uplift that arose out of the January 2025 winter storm in the Northeast––thus undermining the signals that the prices should convey.

[R]ecent extreme winter weather has once again highlighted critical flaws in PJM's market structure, resulting in over $400 million in uplift costs in 2025 year-to-date—expenses that cannot be hedged by load-serving entities through forward energy purchases and which are often passed directly to consumers.
Such after-the-fact adjustments make it difficult for investors to assess the potential viability of electricity projects.
Meeting this growing load will require significant new generation, transmission, and flexible resources—all of which depend on clear and durable RTO-ISO price signals.
ETI recommends that the DOE and the Commission work with the RTO-ISOs to strengthen locational pricing mechanisms to more properly reflect system conditions.
ETI recommends that the DOE use its authorities to prioritize market-based reforms as part of DOE's grid modernization and transmission funding programs.

letters.org: Enerwise Global Technologies, LLC dba CPower
letters.desc: Load flexibility is less expensive than new generation, using simple metering, communication, and thermostat modifications. Costs are low and achievable, making it an economical solution for demand balancing.
quotes: Given this reality, load flexibility – a more readily available resource - must also play a part in enabling the interconnection of large loads. Leveraging load flexibility has a couple of key advantages: it will be quicker to deploy, and it will be less expensive in most cases.

Load flexibility is inexpensive because it is often enabled just by putting in place simple metering and communication mechanisms, or in the case of automated demand response, it can be as straightforward as installing a programmable thermostat. In either case, these solutions are low cost and quickly achievable.

All customers who provide load flexibility should be treated equitably regardless of whether they are participating in legacy ISO/RTO constructs or are providing this flexibility as a new large load customer. Equity should be provided across customer types in terms of payment, performance, order of dispatch, dispatch frequency, and duration of dispatch.

In short, large loads that agree to be curtailable in exchange for an expedited interconnection should, in no case, receive preferential treatment to other types of demand response in the wholesale markets. Such treatment would run afoul of the Federal Power Act, which prohibits wholesale market rates, terms, or conditions that constitute preferential treatment or that are unduly discriminatory.

letters.desc: ENGIE supports cost allocation that tracks actual grid impact: facilities pay for upgrades they cause, netting of co-located generation reduces ancillary service charges, and no crediting mechanism should shift costs to ratepayers.
quotes: Allowing large loads and co-located generation to net meter is the most efficient way to interconnect large loads. Netting of load and generation reduces the need for unnecessary system upgrades and associated costs, and decreases the need for subsidies which reduces ratepayer costs.

ENGIE does not believe that a crediting mechanism is necessary as large load and hybrid interconnection costs should be paid for by the facilities themselves. A credit mechanism may risk shifting costs onto ratepayers.

ENGIE finds this principle is problematic because it ignores the operational reality and fairness considerations of hybrid facilities. If facilities are charged based solely on peak demand, without netting co-located generation, it treats the site as if the generation does not exist.

letters.desc: Entergy supports the principle that large loads pay their full share of upgrade costs but stresses that states retain jurisdiction over how those costs are allocated in retail rate proceedings.
quotes: we agree that the study of load and generation additions together can result in a more efficient and cost-effective identification of transmission upgrades.

the Commission must not impose any rules that could result in large loads paying less than their fair share of transmission costs, which includes the costs that they cause as a result of the need for upgrades or other appropriate transmission system modifications so that these new loads can be safely and securely interconnected.

letters.org: Entergy Services, LLCEntergy New Orleans, LLCEntergy Louisiana, LLC ,Entergy Mississippi, LLC ,Entergy Arkansas, LLC ,Entergy Texas, Inc. ,
letters.desc: Entergy highlights $5 billion in projected customer savings from data center agreements and Arkansas legislation requiring that large load growth keep power affordable, arguing that existing state cost-allocation mechanisms protect retail customers without federal intervention.
quotes: Act 373 is designed to help Entergy Arkansas and other utilities attract large commercial customers.  The statute allows Entergy Arkansas to build the infrastructure needed to support new large load growth, while keeping power affordable and reliable.

Entergy Corporation announced that approximately $5 billion in total savings will accrue to 2.3 million customers in Arkansas, Louisiana, and Mississippi because of data center customer agreements in those states.

letters.desc: ELPC argues that high-voltage connection facilities built solely to serve individual large-load customers are improperly placed into the shared transmission rate base, spreading costs worth billions of dollars annually to existing ratepayers. ELPC supports rules and state tariff approaches that assign those costs directly to the customers who cause them.
quotes: The consequences are higher prices for consumers and regulators at every level facing significant questions as to how to meet electricity demand growth while ensuring affordability and reliability.

large load customers often require new lines and substations at voltages of 138kV or higher. Mr. Jacobs explained that although such high-voltage connection facilities are essentially line extensions that the utility designs to serve a specific customer, the utilities socialize their costs by placing them into the transmission rate base.
