Mr. Jacobs provided his analysis showing that such connection facilities added up to $4.1 billion across PJM in 2024 alone, with costs continuing to increase in 2025 and beyond.

the California Public Utilities Commission recently issued an interim order requiring new transmission-level customers seeking retail services to be responsible for the initial costs of all transmission facilities, rather than those costs being borne by ratepayers.
the Company practices that do provide tracking of these transmission costs are not used to pursue cost allocation that would apply cost-causation principles.

the Company makes decisions regarding functionalization of new facilities as transmission or distribution without any oversight. Such decisions have a major impact on retail rates. ComEd should make these decisions with greater transparency and oversight.
The Company does not plan to use Cluster Studies to assign the costs of new facilities to the Large Demand Project Applicants or Customers that cause those costs.

letters.desc: Eolian argues that the current regime causes existing transmission customers to absorb upgrade costs triggered by large loads, and that enabling flexibility commitments is the primary mechanism to avoid those upgrades and reduce cost shifts. It also supports an expanded and standardized option to build as a tool to lower interconnection costs.
quotes: Flexibility commitments from loads and hybrid resources can help to protect existing customers by avoiding the need for transmission system upgrades and allowing large loads to reduce the resource adequacy impacts of their interconnection and allow large loads—and the resources needed to serve them—to come online quickly without the need for extensive study or network upgrades.

The absence of standardized, transparent procedures creates opportunities for undue discrimination in queue processing and transmission upgrade cost assignment as public utilities negotiate individual contracts with loads.

Eolian has experienced multiple cases where a transmission provider's refusal to perform an integrated study of load and generation has caused duplicative upgrade requirements that could have been avoided if load and generation had been considered together, which has impacted the business viability of both load and generation.

failure to truly enable flexible loads and provide them a means to internalize the benefits they provide to the system could otherwise result in the worst of all worlds: shifting large load interconnection to a standardized federal process that slows down progress by disrupting the potential for state innovation and failing to reduce the monumental cost of transmission expansion and capacity growth otherwise necessary to integrate large loads into the transmission system.
The Commission should build upon its experience in the generator interconnection process by further reducing barriers to use of the option to build.

letters.desc: Eolian supports a Transmission Security Commitment framework as a substitute for direct cost assignment, giving developers predictable rolled-in transmission rates while protecting existing customers through aggregate security sized to network upgrade exposure. It frames cost certainty as critical to enabling bridge solutions and financing for flexible hybrid facilities.
quotes: the record provides a better path to achieving this goal: Transmission Security Commitments to ensure that large load customers, in aggregate, will contribute their fair share to network upgrade costs via rolled-in pricing.

FERC could avoid repeating the problems that have plagued generator interconnection queues through an approach that provides greater up-front cost certainty to interconnection customers, which is the single most powerful tool for reducing speculative and duplicative requests, study complexity, and re-studies.

As a developer of FERC-jurisdictional generation projects, Eolian confirms that under a direct assignment regime, generation developers have no choice but to use the interconnection process as a price discovery mechanism.
such cost certainty will lower overall system costs by reducing risk for project developers

Even if the Commission elects only to provide for expedited interconnection for hybrid facilities rather than providing for a robust implementation of the ANOPR that establishes a standard interconnection process for new large load customers, the Commission should not apply the cost causation framework set forth in principle 8, nor the status quo cost causation framework for generator interconnection.

letters.desc: Eolian contends that uncoordinated studies trigger network upgrade costs that would not arise under integrated processes. SPP's temporary CHILLS and HILLGA programs leave projects exposed to late-stage upgrade assignments, creating commercial risk for both load and generation developers.
quotes: The lack of tariff provisions to afford all three elements results in unjust and unreasonable or unduly discriminatory rates by exacerbating the reliability and affordability impacts of large load growth, while impeding speed-to-power for new large loads.

HILLGA and CHILLS are not permanent service options, interconnection of both load and generation via this process remains subject to network upgrades that may be subsequently identified in the load and generation's permanent interconnection study processes. And such permanent interconnection study process, which occurs under SPP's Consolidated Planning Process, may be years after the facilities are operational. This creates potentially unworkable commercial risks for both load and generation that will inhibit use of these processes

utilities may provide for outcomes that maximize their own return on equity while triggering the construction of infrastructure that would not be needed were the process to more accurately reflect planned system additions.

letters.desc: Equinix argues that costs benefiting only the large load should be borne by that customer, while costs providing broader grid benefit should follow the beneficiary-pays principle. The company also cites empirical evidence that large-load growth has tended to reduce average retail electricity prices.
quotes: [G]rowth in recent years (through 2024) has tended to reduce average retail electricity prices. … states with the highest load growth experienced reductions in real prices, whereas states with contracting loads generally saw prices rise.

where costs incurred provide broader benefit, however, cost allocation should follow the beneficiary pays principle, creating an economic signal that maximizes benefits and minimizes costs for all customers.

letters.desc: esVolta contends that BESS lowers costs for non-large-load ratepayers by smoothing volatile demand profiles (shrinking required network upgrades) and by maximizing use of existing transmission capacity rather than requiring new line builds. Evidence cited includes $750 million in Texas day-ahead market savings over three peak days.
quotes: Absent clear, standardized procedures for large load and hybrid interconnections, transmission providers will continue to rely on ad hoc approaches that risk delaying critical projects, exacerbating reliability concerns, and shifting costs to non-participating customers in ways that are inconsistent with open access and just and reasonable rate requirements.

If an ANOPR is issued, it should seek to include a proposal that articulates core principles, such as studying large loads and hybrid facilities together with generation where practicable, recognizing curtailable and dispatchable configurations (including those supported by BESS) for expedited treatment, and aligning cost responsibility with the specific injection and withdrawal rights requested.

When properly configured, BESS can be dispatched to smooth the net load seen by the transmission system, mitigating sudden spikes and drops in demand and thereby transforming a volatile large load into a more "grid-friendly" net profile.

allowing storage to serve large loads is a cost and time efficient way to maximize the utilization of the existing transmission network more so than increasing the capacity of existing transmission lines, which in the context of expeditiously connecting and serving large loads would be cost and time prohibitive.

letters.desc: ETX supports assigning 100% of network upgrade costs to large loads and hybrid projects and opposes offset crediting mechanisms. It argues that co-location should justify itself through genuinely lower upgrade costs, not through a subsidy.
quotes: Load, Hybrid and/or co-located load and generation facilities should be responsible for 100% of their network upgrade costs.
If a project cannot achieve that through lower network upgrade costs, it should not be incentivized to do so with an off-set crediting mechanism.

letters.desc: Fervo supports cost allocation and crediting mechanisms that fairly reflect the transmission system benefits provided by hybrid geothermal facilities, avoiding cost over-assignment for projects that reduce net flows or improve local reliability.
quotes: Fervo supports clear cost-allocation rules but emphasizes that any cost-allocation framework must recognize when a project's design meaningfully reduces its system impact.

Fervo therefore encourages the Commission to ensure that cost responsibility is applied in a way that reflects actual system benefits and not over-assign costs to hybrids that reduce net flows or improve local reliability.
Where appropriate, crediting mechanisms should remain available to acknowledge these benefits and maintain fair treatment across different project types.

letters.desc: FirstEnergy supports the Commission's long-standing policy of rolling network upgrade costs into transmission rates, arguing this avoids jurisdictional disputes and is already paired with utility-level customer protections. It also contends the option to build has not delivered savings even for generators.
quotes: the ANOPR's suggestion that "load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades that they are assigned through the interconnection studies" threatens to inhibit this goal.

The proposed direct assignment of network upgrade costs to an end-use customer raises thorny jurisdictional issues that will result in years of delay, thereby frustrating efficient and timely data center interconnections.

Rather than risk extended delay due to jurisdictional challenges and other cost allocation battles, the Commission should employ its long-standing rolled-in rate approach for network upgrades in conjunction with facilitating customer protections to ensure that other retail load customers are not adversely affected by large load interconnections.

the Commission should use its traditional rolled-in rate approach to ensure that wholesale transmission customers pay their fair share of network upgrade costs that benefit all customers, and the Commission should allow state regulators and load-serving entities to use tariff and/or agreement provisions at the retail level to ensure that large load customers pay their fair share of retail-level costs.

FirstEnergy views the option to build for generator interconnection customers as a failed tariff mechanism that has not resulted in meaningful value or savings that were expected by independent power producers.

letters.desc: FirstEnergy defends rolled-in rate treatment for network upgrade costs as equitable and tested. It argues direct assignment to retail customers raises federal jurisdiction problems and replicates the withdrawal and restudy cycles that have slowed generator interconnection.
quotes: any federal rules governing the interconnection of large load customers should be narrowly tailored to achieving the Administration's speed to power mandate as quickly, affordably, and efficiently as possible.
there is now significant evidence that Order No. 1000 competitive transmission processes are not having the intended result in terms of either efficiency or cost-effectiveness.

if the Commission were to impose a requirement that 100% of network upgrade costs appear on a particular retail customer's electricity bill, that would arguably improperly usurp the states' jurisdiction over retail sales
mandating direct assignment will likely lead to the same inefficiencies that have plagued the generator interconnection process, such as numerous withdrawal and restudy cycles

The best way to avoid these pitfalls is to use the Commission's long-standing approach that network upgrade costs are rolled in to the transmission owner's rate base and recovered from all wholesale transmission customers proportionally to their load

letters.desc: FirstEnergy supports allocating transmission expansion costs directly to the data center driving the need rather than spreading them across all ratepayers. The proposed two-tier structure has the customer pay its pro-rata share of the existing zonal rate plus an incremental expansion rate that recovers the network upgrades built to serve it, using the same financial parameters as the incumbent rate. After a default fifteen-year term the facilities roll into the integrated rate base, and existing households and small businesses stop subsidizing infrastructure they do not benefit from.
quotes: American households are being asked to pay for transmission infrastructure built to serve hyperscale data centers.

Under the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's current rules, when a utility constructs new high-voltage transmission lines and substations to connect a single new data center, the cost of that infrastructure is spread across all customers in the surrounding region.
The Commission developed a durable solution: a rate-design framework requiring the customer driving the expansion to bear the associated costs while leaving the remainder of the system unaffected.
The magnitude of these costs can readily exceed the same five-percent threshold that originally triggered reform in the natural gas context.
That agreement would be filed with and reviewed by FERC under the same just-and-reasonable standard applicable to other jurisdictional transmission arrangements.

The agreement would obligate the data center customer to pay two distinct rate components. First, the customer would pay its standard pro-rata share of the existing zonal transmission rate, applying the same tariff structure applicable to all transmission customers within the zone. Second, the customer would pay an expansion rate specifically designed to recover the costs of the network upgrades required to support the interconnection.

The transmission owner's return on equity, capital structure, and debt assumptions would mirror those already embedded in the incumbent zonal transmission rate, thereby avoiding either preferential treatment or punitive pricing.

To protect existing customers from residual exposure, the data center developer would also maintain creditworthy collateral support equal to the remaining unrecovered balance of the expansion facilities over the life of the agreement.
At the conclusion of the term, the expansion facilities—having been fully recovered—would transition into the integrated system rate base.
Households and small businesses would no longer be required to subsidize infrastructure developed primarily to serve hyperscale facilities.
An expansion-rate framework resolves that tension by providing a clear, FERC-approved path to cost recovery while protecting the existing customer base.

letters.desc: Fluence contends that the final rule should allow storage to charge without triggering network upgrade requirements, reducing interconnection costs for large loads and avoiding delays that undermine the value of BESS.
quotes: the Commission should ensure any final action allows storage resources to charge will not trigger the need for upgrades.

If unreasonable assumptions are applied to BESS that result in unnecessary and lengthy study processes, it will limit large loads from benefiting from the optionality that BESS can provide, which will ultimately exacerbate interconnection delays as opposed to quickening the pace of interconnection.

letters.org: Georgia Power CompanyAlabama Power CompanyMississippi Power Company ,
letters.desc: Southern Companies argue that a workable cost allocation balance, where large loads pay full costs and existing customers are protected, is achievable and has already been demonstrated in Georgia, Alabama, and Mississippi. They support this approach as a national model but oppose any federal rule that would override state retail ratemaking to impose a different standard.
quotes: Southern Companies wholeheartedly endorse the ANOPR's stated objective of ensuring "timely and orderly interconnection of large loads to the transmission system."

Doing so in a manner that ensures the reliability of the grid and appropriately allocates costs across customer classes is also crucially important to ensure the fast-moving nature of this demand growth does not create an undue risk that existing retail customers would subsidize a large load that seeks interconnection.

A combination of minimum bill requirements, termination provisions, and longer contract terms can help to ensure that data centers and other large load customers pay the full cost of serving them and avoid any risk that existing retail customers, particularly working families, seniors and small businesses, will be left to bear the costs.
large load customers acknowledge the demands they place on existing infrastructure and are willing to pay their share of generation and transmission costs in exchange for timely service.

the eighth reform principle, which suggests a new federal standard for how transmission costs should be allocated to large load retail customers, risks directly intruding on retail ratemaking in jurisdictions that have retained bundled retail service.

letters.desc: The GPSC supports requiring large loads to pay their full cost of service. It adopted tariff changes in 2025 requiring customers over 100 MW to meet minimum billing requirements and sign long-term contracts with early termination fees, so existing customers are not burdened by new load costs.
quotes: the GPSC has the authority and flexibility to facilitate this growth in a manner that will meet the electricity needs of new customers while protecting existing customers from upward pressure on utility rates.

the GPSC has acted in the past year to further solidify its regulatory mandate in response to the timely and orderly interconnection of large loads. In April 2025 the Commission approved changes to its rules and regulations requiring Georgia Power to ensure that new customers over 100 MW pay their cost of service through minimum billing requirements, long term contracts with sizable fees in the case of early termination, and other terms and conditions

letters.desc: The filing strongly backs assigning costs based on each load's net grid impact, consistent with the cost causation principle, and opposes assessments that charge co-located hybrid facilities for transmission or ancillary services beyond their actual withdrawal commitments.
quotes: Geronimo Power fully agrees with this principle because assessing large loads transmission service charges based upon their actual withdrawal rights appropriately limits the cost responsibility of such customers to the costs necessary to provide them with the service requested.

The cost causation principle requires that 'all approved rates reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who must pay them' and prohibits the Commission from approving a rate scheme that will result in one group of customers being required to subsidize the provision of service to a different group of customers.
Assessing large loads based on their net impact is not only required by the cost causation principle, it will also accelerate the ability of large loads to obtain power on a timely basis.

principle twelve of the ANOPR states that 'utilities serving large loads, including those at hybrid facilities, should be responsible for ancillary services based on peak demand, without consideration of any co-located generation.'

A better approach for the Commission to take is to treat ancillary service costs in the same manner as it has proposed to treat transmission service charges: large loads pay for ancillary services based on their actual use of, and reliance on, the service at issue.

letters.desc: Google supports the principle that transmission service charges should be based on a large load's actual withdrawal rights from the grid, not its theoretical peak demand. This aligns with the Commission's long-standing cost causation precedent and is especially relevant for co-located configurations where the generator may serve the load behind the meter.
quotes: Google agrees with the principle that the transmission service used to provide energy to new large loads should be based on the specific use of the transmission system at that point of interconnection.

To comport with the cost causation principle that undergirds the just and reasonable standard, a load's transmission service should be measured based on its actual withdrawal rights from the transmission system.

letters.desc: Google supports sizing network upgrades and transmission service based on actual injection and withdrawal rights rather than gross load. This approach sends better price signals to developers and reduces unnecessary upgrade costs for ratepayers.
quotes: Inadequate electric transmission infrastructure is becoming the principal limitation to interconnecting new large loads, including data centers, and the needed generation capacity at the speed and scale necessary to sustain our global economic competitiveness.
it takes too long to interconnect new large loads and new generation, and the cost of doing so is too high. Lengthy interconnection delays are directly driving up energy prices.

Determining what network upgrades are required to accommodate the actual injection and withdrawal rights requested and providing transmission service based on the actual use of the transmission system will send the proper signals to encourage developers to pursue the most efficient projects.

letters.org: Governor Josh Shapiro and Governor Glenn Youngkin
letters.desc: The governors support the framework's requirement that LLAs take responsibility for their network upgrade costs and note that inaccurate forecasts risk overbuild that drives up costs for consumers.
quotes: this framework would provide strong incentives for LLAs to invest in nearby new energy generation and storage resources, to curtail during tight market conditions, and to take responsibility for their network upgrade costs.

some recent load forecasts have markedly exceeded real-world constraints on load construction, such as the available supply of semiconductor chips, risking significant overbuild and associated cost increases for consumers.

letters.desc: GridCARE contends that better identification of latent capacity and more precise load characterization can reduce unnecessary upgrade costs for existing customers. The company also supports tiered study fees and performance incentives for transmission providers as tools to align costs with system benefits.
quotes: planners can underestimate the hosting capacity that exists across the vast majority of hours. This gap between actual operational conditions and modeling assumptions contributes to the perception that only long-lead infrastructure can serve new load, when in many cases the constraint may be limited to a small number of hours or conditions.

Systematically incorporating this flexibility ecosystem into planning and operations will unlock existing capacity on the grid, accelerate interconnections, and enable beneficial load growth to preserve customer affordability and fund new infrastructure investment.
Applying generator-level deliverability assumptions to non-export configurations can overstate impacts, increase upgrade requirements, and erode the very flexibility the ANOPR seeks to unlock.

the Commission should establish a load-interconnection study-fee framework that scales with the size and complexity of the proposed load and reflects the level of operational flexibility demonstrated by the customer.
the Commission should consider performance-based incentives for transmission providers tied to each megawatt of load interconnected on an accelerated or performance-defined timeline.

A framework that better utilizes existing assets can serve near-term load, maintain affordability, and support the investment environment for utilities while long-lead projects progress through permitting and construction.

letters.desc: GridStor states that upgrades identified for ESR charging should be allocated under the same established cost-allocation principles applied to other interconnection upgrades.
quotes: Such upgrades would be allocated following the established cost-allocation principles applied to other interconnection upgrades.

letters.desc: Harvard ELI argues that ratepayers bear both short-term subsidy risk (when a large-load customer pays only NITS and departs before the crossover point) and long-term free-rider risk (when a customer pays only upgrade costs and never contributes to embedded system costs). The filing supports pricing that recovers both network upgrade costs and the NITS rate from large-load customers to eliminate both failure modes.
quotes: WIRES' analysis shows that ratepayers face increased costs and risks under either rolled-in pricing or direct assignment of network upgrade costs
Because the NITS rate does not recover from the large-load customer the costs its interconnection directly imposes on other ratepayers, ratepayers initially subsidize the large-load customer.
If the large-load customer paying the NITS rate departs the system before the crossover point, the only cost shift that would have materialized runs from ratepayers to the large-load customer.
Despite relying on the network, the large-load customer pays nothing for its ongoing development, replacement, maintenance, or operations.
Payments for network upgrades and the NITS rate, the Commission concluded, were two 'separate charges for separate services.'
Under either approach, the utility would directly assign network upgrade costs to the large-load customer and charge the NITS rate.
Rather than merely allowing the utility to charge the 'higher of' rate for each tranche, the Commission could require utilities to charge the higher rate.

After the Commission modifies its transmission pricing policy to exempt large-load customers from the prohibition against 'and' pricing, the Commission could find that any transmission rate charging a large-load customer less than the cost of network upgrades and the NITS rate is unjust and unreasonable.

The Commission should extend that reasoning and clarify that just and reasonable rates for large-load customers must recover both the customer-specific interconnection costs and the customer's share of the embedded system.

letters.desc: Helion argues that collocated generation reduces stress on shared grid infrastructure and addresses both interconnection and capacity challenges simultaneously, implicitly supporting cost allocation that recognizes these benefits.
quotes: When baseload, dispatchable, non-fuel-limited generation is collocated with large loads, both the interconnection challenge and the generation/transmission capacity challenge can be addressed simultaneously.

letters.desc: Heron argues performance-based rules lower costs for ratepayers, and that cost-causation under Principle 8 should run symmetrically so grid-forming loads' system benefits are credited against direct-assignment network upgrade costs.
quotes: Overly prescriptive rules with generation mandates or lengthy interconnection studies that fail to recognize the capabilities of modern power electronics to support the grid will produce longer queue timelines, higher costs, and more network upgrades.
Where energy-integrated power electronics can satisfy the same performance requirements at lower cost, ratepayers benefit.
the Commission should direct RTOs and transmission owners to credit the grid services provided by grid-forming large loads against any direct-assignment network upgrade costs.
The cost-causation principle underlying ANOPR Principle 8 should apply symmetrically to benefits as well as costs.

letters.desc: The filing documents dramatic wholesale price increases in PJM and MISO attributable to large load growth, and argues that all system upgrade costs must fall on the large load through CIAC, not be socialized across ratepayers or recovered through a crediting mechanism.
quotes: In PJM capacity prices effective June 1, 2025 skyrocketed by approximately 833% increasing from $28.92 per MW-day to $269.92 per MW-day, and further increased to $329.17 per MW-day for 2026-2027.
In the MISO area the summer capacity price increased by an astonishing $635 per MW-day, or approximately 2,122%, from $30 MW-day to $666.50 MW-day.

large load projects create significant risks, including the risks of: (1) insufficient supply to meet existing demand and the additional demand of large load projects, (2) skyrocketing prices both in response to insufficient supply and to provide "incentives" in the hope that increased generator revenues will cause them to build sufficient generation to meet the large load demand, and (3) electricity shortages leading to blackouts or "load shed."

Adopting clear rules on the interconnection of large loads to the transmission system is necessary to address the effect that these outsized loads have on the wholesale electricity markets and on the transmission system and to prevent practices that will lead to unjust and unreasonable cost shifts and prices.

New load and generation may be sited at the same point of interconnection (i.e. hybrid facilities), but to minimize costs on the transmission system they should be sited within the smallest applicable market area even if they are not at the same point of interconnection.

new large load contracts with generators who currently serve the aggregate load of electricity customers throughout the country, from residential customers to major industrial load, will siphon power from the grid and leave customers who rely on the bulk power system vulnerable to scarcity pricing and possible shortages and blackouts.
The costs of large load, hybrid facilities, and associated generation should be paid exclusively by the large load seeking to connect to the system.

Requiring a large load customer to pay all installation and upgrade costs ensures that the cost-causer pays for the system upgrade. This prevents socialization of system costs that do not benefit the breadth of ratepayers and prevents stranding the costs of the upgrade if the customer's business fails.
when customers pay the full cost that they impose on the system through a CIAC payment, it is not necessary to use a crediting mechanism to cover those costs.

letters.desc: The filer strongly supports rolled-in cost allocation as the default for network upgrades triggered by large load interconnections, citing longstanding Commission precedent. They argue that direct assignment of 100% of costs would provoke years of cost-allocation litigation, raise jurisdictional problems, and ultimately increase costs for other retail customers. Utilities and data centers are already developing bilateral agreements that protect ratepayers without mandating direct assignment.
quotes: Costs of transmission network upgrades triggered by interconnection of large load customers should, by default, be rolled into transmission rates consistent with longstanding Commission precedent on the treatment of integrated transmission facilities, rather than directly assigned to individual customers.

Rolled-in rate treatment will promote more efficient and timely large load interconnection by avoiding cost allocation and jurisdictional disputes, as well as ensuring that all load customers continue to contribute their fair share of the benefits of an integrated transmission network.
the Commission should bolster those efforts with an even-handed, across-the-board wholesale cost allocation to give the states a clean slate upon which to make retail rate determinations.
regardless of how the Commission decides to allocate the costs of network upgrades, it must consider how the effect of its action or inaction affects all customers—not just large load customers.

a federal requirement to assign 100 percent of transmission network upgrade costs to a particular end-use retail customer (the large load customer) . . . would eliminate the states' traditional authority to regulate how the utility allocates its total transmission costs among various retail customer rate classes and would be beyond the authority granted to the Commission by the United States Congress.

the Commission should use that jurisdiction to require that costs benefiting the transmission network be rolled into the transmission providers' rate base and recovered, with a reasonable rate of return, from all network transmission customers.

letters.desc: The filer strongly supports preserving rolled-in rate treatment and encourages service agreements with consumer protection terms as the vehicle for managing cost shifts, rather than direct assignment or holding wholesale entities responsible for a single customer's upgrade costs.
quotes: A number of commenters indicate support for direct assignment of network transmission upgrade costs to large load customers, claiming that doing so best comports with cost causation principles.  Their assertions are wrong and contrary to decades of Commission precedent governing transmission pricing policy.

transmission upgrades, even when prompted in whole or part by data center interconnections can, and often do, involve significant work on integrated facilities that serve customers across wide geographic areas.

Direct assignment of network upgrade costs dramatically increases the costs to the data center and will likely reduce the number of data centers that interconnect and slow others that are sufficiently brave to weather the process.

the better approach, and one that avoids protracted cost allocation disputes, as well as better respects jurisdictional boundaries, is to continue to apply the Commission's longstanding preference for rolled-in rate treatment as the default cost allocation methodology for large load driven network upgrades.
the Commission should instead consider encouraging transmission providers to develop and submit for filing large load service agreements that contain comprehensive customer protection mechanisms

letters.desc: Demand reduction via cool-roof technology costs far less than building new generation capacity. Large users should fund these programs as the direct cause of grid costs under cost-causation principles.
quotes: The cost of demand reduction would be pennies on the dollar compared to the cost of new generation.

My proposal is simple. The data centers and other large users should be required, as a condition of interconnection, to secure a commensurate amount of demand reduction to the amount of load they plan to put onto the grid. This would be consistent with the ratemaking principle of 'cost causation.'

letters.desc: The filer concludes that data centers should continue to fund the interconnection upgrades their load requires rather than receiving offset credit based on regional VPP statistics.
quotes: VPPs should continue to receive appropriate compensation through capacity markets for their genuine Resource Adequacy contributions. Data centers should continue to fund interconnection upgrades necessary to maintain physical system reliability.

letters.desc: Hopkins argues that data center demand has directly caused her electric bill to more than double since 2021, backed by PJM market monitor figures attributing most of the capacity price surge to data centers. She asks FERC to require large commercial loads to bear the full cost of their interconnection infrastructure rather than spreading those costs to residential ratepayers, and frames the current practice as a violation of the Federal Power Act's just and reasonable standard.
quotes: my electric bill is proof of the unfair and systematic transfer of costs from large commercial electricity consumers to residential ratepayers.
Penelec's residential Price to Compare has increased from 4.981 cents per kWh in March 2021 to 11.747 cents per kWh in December 2025.
The PJM independent market monitor has attributed 63% of the 833% capacity auction price increase between the 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 delivery years to data center electricity demand.
This translates to $9.3 billion in costs being paid by 67 million ratepayers across the 13 PJM states.
Any jobs, tax revenue, and economic activity created by those facilities remain in Virginia and Maryland, but the costs are socialized onto me and the other millions of ratepayers in PJM states.

require that large loads, specifically data centers and other high-density commercial facilities, bear the full cost of transmission infrastructure required to interconnect them to the interstate transmission system, rather than socializing those costs across existing ratepayer classes.

require that PJM's capacity auction cost allocation methodology distinguish between infrastructure serving broad public load and infrastructure serving concentrated private commercial loads. The current framework treats these identically. They are not identical.

Requiring residential ratepayers in rural Pennsylvania to subsidize the electricity infrastructure of Fortune 500 technology companies generating no local economic benefit is neither just nor reasonable.

letters.desc: The filer supports placing localized upgrade costs on the party whose siting decision creates them, through node-level demand caps and stiff-point qualification requirements. Under the current framework, ratepayers absorb upgrade costs from siting decisions they had no role in. Demand caps that halt approvals once node capacity is committed force developers to fund upgrades or choose qualifying sites.
quotes: The requirement that large-load interconnection applicants demonstrate node adequacy, or fund the specific localized upgrades required to achieve it, places network optimization costs on the party whose siting decision creates them.

A demand cap that halts new interconnection approvals at a node once its available capacity has been committed forces the next developer to either identify a different node, fund the upgrade required to expand capacity at the chosen node, or wait until existing load is reduced. In each case, the cost of the siting decision is borne by the party making it.

PJM, MISO, SPP, and other RTOs and ISOs operating under FERC jurisdiction should file tariff amendments implementing node-level demand caps for large-load interconnection. Caps should be set at the fault-level capacity available at each interconnection point, net of existing committed load.

letters.org: Industrial Energy Consumers of America et al.
letters.desc: The filers argue that rate-base incentives systematically push transmission owners toward new construction over cost-effective optimization. They want FERC to enforce the cost causation principle, refine it for small-denominator utility zones vulnerable to cost shifts, and create non-recovery risk for owners who skip GETs evaluation.
quotes: To unleash the ANOPR's speed-to-power objectives, the Commission should narrowly focus its near-term efforts on optimizing existing system capacity (or transfer capability) via reconductoring and deployment of GETs and require the transparency of load forecasting and assumptions underlying transmission system studies.
the Commission must address head-on the underlying financial incentive for transmission owners to understate system capability to overbuild and expand rate base

the Commission could establish a risk of non-recovery of the costs of new transmission facilities that are placed into service if transmission owner fails to consider GETs or advanced technology alternatives to the new construction.

the Commission must protect customers by upholding the cost causation principle, and as necessary, refine the application of that principle to account for instances where existing customers may be more vulnerable to cost shifts associated with a large new load in a smaller utility zone

letters.desc: ITI supports the principle that loads bear 100% of upgrade costs directly triggered by their interconnection, but when regional upgrades provide broader benefits, costs should be allocated according to benefits, following the beneficiary pays principle in Order 1920/1920-A.
quotes: ITI supports the principle that large loads should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades assigned through the interconnection study results. However, large-scale regional network upgrades, such as those planned through regional transmission planning processes, spread a wide range of benefits to a wide range of customers. Large loads should be responsible for 100% of the upgrades directly triggered by their interconnection to the extent that those upgrades do not convey broader benefit to other grid customers. On the other hand, when upgrades do provide broader benefits, costs should be allocated in accordance with their benefits.
Any rulemaking by the Commission should maintain consistent 'beneficiary pays' cost allocation principles, as directed by Order 1920/1920-A.

letters.desc: iMasons consistently invokes the Commission's cost causation principle to argue that deposits, penalties, upgrade cost assignments, and revenue guarantees must all be tied to costs that large load customers actually cause. Revenue guarantee constructs like Exelon's TSA framework are singled out as violations of this principle.
quotes: the lack of coordination with regard to large load interconnection processes leads to inaccurate load forecasts, resulting in, among other things, the inefficient buildout of generation and transmission to serve load.
Deposits and penalties should be fashioned in a manner that mitigates risks and costs that large loads actually pose to transmission owners and other customers.

Requirements that are disproportionate to the risk and costs that large loads actually pose to transmission owners and other customers do not help protect consumers, and instead, overcompensate utilities and risk stifling the market for data centers in the United States.

the TSA construct, and any similar 'revenue guarantee' proposals that may be proposed by other transmission owners, would clearly run afoul of the Commission's cost causation principal, which requires 'that all approved rates reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer [that] must pay them.'
the Commission should not permit utilities to 'claw back' capacity that has already been secured by a large load developer or hyperscale end-user.

Encouraging hybrid facilities will help solve 'speed to power' issues for data centers, enhance reliability by encouraging data centers to bring their own generation when they interconnect and can alleviate the need for building excess network upgrades, which will benefit consumers.

iMasons encourages the Commission to promulgate a final rule that would require large load customers to be allocated only costs that they cause, consistent with the Commission's longstanding cost causation principles.

letters.desc: IFP supports assigning 100% of network upgrade costs to the interconnecting large load. This approach is justified because large loads are well capitalized, and clear cost allocation provides the financial certainty developers and investors need for multi-billion dollar projects.
quotes: Principle 8 proposes that large loads should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades assigned to them. This is appropriate because – though it places an additional financial burden on the large loads – such loads are well capitalized and this cost is small compared to the overall costs of their projects.
allocating responsibility in this way provides the cost certainty that developers, and their investors, critically need to finance multi-billion dollar projects.

letters.desc: IECA endorses full cost responsibility for interconnecting parties, consistent with the generator cost allocation model, with grid benefits from new generation recognized as offsets.
quotes: we support requiring load and hybrid facilities, including any associated electric generating facilities not sharing an interconnection point with its associated Data Center, to bear all the costs of network upgrades required for their interconnection(s) and we support offsetting such costs through a crediting mechanism as is applicable under the Commissions interconnection rules applicable to generators.

letters.desc: IECA supports placing interconnection and study costs on large load developers, consistent with how generator interconnection costs are allocated today. This approach puts stranded-investment risk on parties best positioned to manage it.
quotes: we also support having the costs of interconnections of large loads, including the costs of all necessary system impact studies, be borne by the developers and customers of such large loads, which should place the risk of stranded investment on those in the best position to manage such risk, i.e., the developers of such large loads.

letters.org: Invenergy Wind Development North America LLCInvenergy Solar Development North America LLCInvenergy Thermal Development Holdings LLC ,
letters.desc: Invenergy argues that security deposits, study deposits, and network upgrade cost allocation must follow cost-causation principles. Arbitrary multi-billion-dollar security demands untethered to actual upgrade costs block viable projects and favor incumbents. Right-sized deposits would free capital for generation and load development.
quotes: the existence of disparate rules in each jurisdiction incentivizes large load customers to forum shop for the best rules by submitting interconnection requests in multiple service territories, thereby inducing speculative interconnection requests and increasing systemwide costs.

transmission owners too often require developers to post billions of dollars in security up front to interconnect hybrid facilities without any regard to the actual cost of interconnecting and serving data center load, in some instances requiring hybrid projects to securitize both the load and generation interconnection requests.
studying load and generation separately can, and often does, result in the identification of network upgrades that would not be needed had the facilities been studied together.

study deposits for large load and hybrid facilities should be based on the size of the request. For hybrid interconnection requests, there should be only one study deposit that is based on the greater of the generation size or load size, but not both.

Any commercial readiness or security required should be determined based on the amount of the network upgrades required to interconnect the load, consistent with the generator interconnection rules and the Commission's cost causation policy.

Invenergy agrees with DOE's proposal to make load and hybrid facilities responsible for 100% of the network upgrades that they are assigned through any interconnection studies, rather than allocate such costs to non-large load customers or generators in the interconnection queue.
hybrid projects should be studied as one project for purposes of assigning network upgrade costs, rather than studying the load and generation separately.

letters.desc: Federal regulation should enable fair cost allocation across customer classes, with large loads paying directly for transmission and generation investments rather than posting collateral, improving capital efficiency and derisking utilities.
quotes: If done correctly, facilitating large loads to interconnect under federal regulation would provide efficient and cost-effective processes that result in fair cost allocation for all electric customers.
Focus on cost allocation that is fair for all.

Allowing large load customers to directly pay for these transmission and generation investments would provide a more efficient use of capital while at the same time also derisking utilities and other load serving entities.

The proposed ANOPR could be improved by allowing large load customers to pay directly for improvements on the interstate transmission grid, including GETs, instead of having these costs recovered through retail utility minimum demand charges or other tariff mechanisms that limit the utilization of these investments.

letters.desc: ISO-NE supports allocating upgrade costs to the requesting load or hybrid facility and wants the cost assignment method and any crediting mechanism to be simple. It cautions against study scope creep that could trigger restudies and redistribute costs.
quotes: The principle should also establish that upgrades identified in the Cluster Studies (and the corresponding cost responsibility for such upgrades) will be limited to the requests for projects that were part of the same Cluster that included the load and/or hybrid facility.   Without this limitation, there could be a potential increase of restudies of previously completed Cluster Studies.

ISO-NE agrees with the principle that load and hybrid facilities should be fully responsible for upgrades needed to support their interconnections.  This construct exists today for RNS.  The methodology used to assign responsibility for upgrades and any crediting mechanism should be simple.

letters.desc: ITC emphasizes that utilities are entitled to full cost recovery and reasonable returns on prudent investments regardless of cost allocation mechanisms employed. Benefits from system upgrades accrue broadly and should support broad-based cost allocation rather than placing burden on individual projects.
quotes: Transmission system upgrades driven by large load additions can enhance system reliability, reduce congestion, and enable future generator and load integration. Of course, these benefits accrue system-wide, making it reasonable for utilities to recover costs through transmission rates rather than imposing disproportionate burdens on individual projects.

if the Commission pursues any untested cost allocation approaches to accommodate the aggressive timing and size requirements of large loads, FERC must recognize and implement a foundational principle of the regulatory compact: public utilities are entitled to recover their costs and earn a reasonable return on prudent investments made to provide FERC jurisdictional service.

Utility shareholders should not be forced to subsidize network upgrades or any other transmission system investment without a return on those investments. Utilities must be able to attract capital to facilitate these large load interconnections, and that requires a fair return on that capital.

letters.desc: ITC advocates that large loads must bear network transmission service charges to avoid cost shifts to existing ratepayers. The filer argues this approach is essential for enabling rate reductions over time; ITC Midwest projects a 20% transmission rate decrease by decade's end as data center loads expand the customer base sharing fixed network costs.
quotes: ITC supports the Commission's efforts to evaluate and identify potential reforms to ensure large loads can interconnect quickly and reliably while avoiding cost shifts to existing customers.

current regulatory frameworks, including large loads' obligations to pay for the ongoing development, maintenance, and operation of the overall transmission system through network transmission service charges, accomplish these goals when paired with proactive transmission planning, the knowledge of local Transmission Owners, and other policies that promote optimal long-term solutions over quick or narrowly focused fixes.
large loads is projected to progressively reduce transmission rates for customers by expanding the load base over which fixed network costs are recovered.
by the end of the decade, the network transmission rate for ITC Midwest's customers is anticipated to decrease by approximately 20% from the 2026 projected rate.

a key precondition to capturing these benefits is for large loads to be assigned network transmission service charges. Without including large loads in the network transmission service charge calculation, customers would bear severe cost shifts and not reap the associated rate benefits these loads provide for all customers.

letters.desc: The KCC strongly supports protecting existing customers from cost shifts caused by large load interconnection. It points to Kansas's LLPS tariff as a model, but argues federal cost allocation reforms tied to regional transmission planning are also needed because state tools cannot reach wholesale regional upgrade costs.
quotes: the KCC approved a unanimous settlement agreement that will establish a new Large Load Power Service ("LLPS") rate plan that is designed to serve electric customers that reasonably expect to need a peak load of at least 75 MW

The minimum bill calculation includes payment of a reasonable allocation of all transmission costs incurred by the retail utility to serve retail customers, including network upgrades constructed as a result of interconnection studies or other regional transmission expansion plans.

the focus on cost allocation within interconnection studies is misplaced. The larger issue is the cost increases and potential cost shifts associated with regional transmission expansion plans, which states do not have authority to fully address.
there is currently no mechanism under federal statutes or regulations that require projected loads to commit to pay for the regional projects ahead of building those projects

the KCC notes the harm that traditional loads would be subjected to if the large loads that formed the basis for the transmission plans do not materialize, leaving only existing customers to pay for generational expansions of the transmission grid

letters.desc: The Alliance recommends that new large-load facilities pay for transmission upgrades they require rather than passing those costs to existing ratepayers. It also warns that overbuilt infrastructure from inflated demand forecasts would saddle ordinary customers with stranded-asset costs.
quotes: the waste of the billions of taxpayer dollars that funded the acquisition of these conservation protections.
if the projected data center load fails to fully materialize, then the cost of these assets — whether power plants or pipeline infrastructure — would be borne by other utility customers.

Placing the costs of upgrading transmission infrastructure on new large load users, such as data centers, and not on pre-existing customers, will likely reduce strain on the grid, as large load facilities would be incentivized to minimize their energy consumption.

letters.desc: LPPC consistently insists that large load must bear all incremental costs it causes, including generation investment, distribution upgrades, and network upgrades, and that state regulators must retain authority to enforce this through tariffs and contract terms.
quotes: LPPC asks the Commission to clarify that the ANOPR's disclaimer reserving authority to states encompasses not only rates for direct retail sales but also the ability of Load Serving Entities ("LSEs") to assess the cost of new generation needed to serve large data centers at the outset of service, and to require contractual commitments of specified length to assure cost recovery.

The Commission should expressly hold that its intention is not to preempt the exercise of state authority over the terms of retail service to large load, including the allocation of generation, distribution upgrade costs, retail contract length, and security requirements.

LPPC agrees that load and hybrid facilities should be fully responsible for network upgrades. No credits or refunds should be required, consistent with the principle of assessing costs to cost causers. Large load interconnections of the magnitude contemplated in many parts of the nation hold the potential for substantial cost shifts to existing load.

letters.desc: LPPC stresses that its members use tariffs, special contracts, customer-funded infrastructure, take-or-pay provisions, minimum billing demand charges, and exit fees to ensure large loads pay their fair share and do not burden existing ratepayers. It presents these as proven mechanisms already protecting everyday customers.
quotes: its member utilities have long employed public power tariffs, special contracts, and bilateral service agreements to integrate large loads while protecting all customers from undue cost-
a summary of the tariff and contractual frameworks those utilities are using to ensure large load customers pay their fair share

LPPC member utilities are employing a variety of customer-protective mechanisms, including dedicated substations, upfront infrastructure funding requirements, take-or-pay provisions, minimum billing demand charges, exit fees, and bring-your-own-power arrangements, to ensure large load growth does not burden existing ratepayers.
Requires the large load customer to pay upfront for dedicated substations, distribution upgrades, transmission lines, and other required facilities.
Bills the customer at a minimum demand level (e.g., fixed percentage of expected peak demand), even if actual usage falls short.

letters.desc: Longroad urges the Commission to reinstate a crediting mechanism modeled on Order No. 2003, under which load and generation are reimbursed after backstop-funding network upgrades. Participant funding has eliminated the transmission owner's incentive to optimize solutions and undermined the beneficiary-pays principle.
quotes: Upgrade costs for generation that are unnecessarily costly have prevented generation from being built, which delays service to large loads.

Longroad urges the Commission to adopt a crediting mechanism. Load and generation would provide backstop security or funds to enable the interconnecting transmission owner to build any required network upgrades following what the Commission adopted in Order No. 2003, and then the load and generation would be reimbursed via credits or cash.

Transmission customers and load clearly benefit as the Commission found in Order No. 2003 and related cases because of the integrated nature of the network upgrades. Reimbursement effectuates that reality.

Another byproduct of the Commission's move away from the Order No. 2003 reimbursement paradigm and moving to participant funding has been removal of the incentive for the public utility transmission provider to optimize transmission planning.

letters.desc: LS Power urges FERC to use competitive processes for network upgrades above 100 kV identified through the interconnection process, and to allow interconnection customers to assign or compete build rights to qualified transmission developers. All infrastructure must receive just and reasonable compensation to attract long-term capital.
quotes: when a new large load requires system or network upgrades, the new large load customer should bear ultimate cost responsibility consistent with cost causation and beneficiary pays principles.

Attracting the long-term capital needed to meet the infrastructure needs created by the surge in large-load demand requires that all infrastructure investments receive just and reasonable compensation, established to the maximum possible extent through independent planning and competition.

letters.org: Maine Office of the Public Advocate
letters.desc: Maine OPA strongly supports requiring large loads to bear the full cost of network upgrades they trigger. The filer explicitly opposes any crediting mechanism that would transfer upgrade costs to existing ratepayers.
quotes: the Maine OPA urges the Commission to proceed with caution to ensure that any final rule protects existing ratepayers by requiring large loads to bear the full cost of necessary network upgrades, by respecting existing state jurisdiction over transactions that are fundamentally retail in nature, and by including provisions that minimize any adverse impacts on wholesale market prices and transmission rates from large load interconnection.
load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades that they are assigned through interconnection studies.

Any crediting mechanism, by necessity, results in the interconnecting entity being relieved of bearing 100% of cost of network upgrades, thus transferring the cost responsibility for the upgrades to other ratepayers.

letters.desc: Maryland emphasizes that large load customers must pay 100% of network upgrade costs assigned to them and opposes cost-shifting to other retail customers. Fair allocation reflects Maryland's law requiring large load tariffs to protect residential customers from financial risk, and addresses real consumer costs from interconnection delays.
quotes: ensure that large load interconnections do not compromise grid reliability or impose undue costs on retail customers
Interconnection bottlenecks impart real costs for Maryland consumers
load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades that they are assigned through the interconnection studies
MEA urges fair allocation of electricity system costs to large load customers, which can prevent unfair shifting of costs to other customers

letters.desc: The Maryland PSC uses PJM IMM data to show that adding large load without new supply can raise Maryland capacity prices by 47% and day-ahead energy prices by 28% to 115%. It supports full cost-causation assignment and opposes any framework that shifts those costs onto existing customers.
quotes: Bringing new (large) load on simultaneously with a matching amount of new generation/storage would maintain the supply/demand balance existing on the grid, thus causing minimal impact to the marginal cost of energy and capacity and lessening the need for network upgrades.

According to the IMM, removing 10,000 MW of nuclear generation in the entire PJM footprint would have increased capacity prices in the state of Maryland by approximately 47% ($526 million) relative to the 2025/2026 Base Residual Auction ("BRA") results.

The Maryland PSC supports the principle of cost allocation on the basis of cost causation, and would emphasize that the total impact to grid reliability caused by a new large load or hybrid facility should be fully represented in the costs that they are assigned through interconnection studies.

Existing generation currently serving customers should not be allowed to suspend their existing service, in whole or in part, simply to serve new large load. Such a suspension would have an adverse impact on cost and raise energy prices.

letters.org: Massachusetts Office of the Attorney General
letters.desc: The filing makes cost protection the central ratepayer ask: full and direct cost assignment, including indirect costs, plus financial safeguards against abandonment. The filers stress that ratepayers already face rising energy costs and cannot absorb new burdens from large load interconnection.
quotes: the State Entities are encouraged by the ANOPR's inclusion of ratepayer protection principles, including that "[l]oad and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades they are assigned."

this rulemaking must include provisions that mitigate the risk of ratepayer subsidization of large load interconnection, including by ensuring that the above cost assignment principle includes a robust assessment that assigns all costs caused by large loads (both direct and indirect) to those same large load customers.

The Commission's rulemaking should also include protections that shield ratepayers from cost risk associated with large load customers that fail to materialize, abandon interconnecting projects, or prematurely exit the transmission system.

letters.desc: The filer documents that shallow charges shift billions in upgrade costs to existing ratepayers, raising bills and stoking opposition. It supports deep charging and bespoke contract structures that place costs on the connecting data centre while providing cost certainty for developers.
quotes: socialising connection charges ("shallow charges") means that the connecting party (i.e. a data centre) does not pay the full cost of the network upgrades, so these are instead borne by other grid users (e.g. residential users).

customers from Illinois, Maryland, New Jersey, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia and West Virginia, collectively paid over US$ 4.3 billion in 2024 for grid investments that were only necessary to accommodate new data centres.

While shallow connection charges can help attract new data centre projects, they can have a negative impact in the local community's cost of living, which could then fuel counter-productive opposition.
Going in the opposite direction, Norway established in their latest policy update that a deep connection charge would be used for projects with capacity above 1 MW.

Data centres could negotiate bespoke contracts with network owners and/or operators, under regulatory approval. These contracts could be used to get the data centres to contribute to the local network to the best of its ability and could result in lower costs for the energy company and lower risks for other grid users.

letters.desc: Meta calls for cost-allocation principles that ensure no negative grid reliability impacts or unfair cost shifts to other customers when generation powering large loads is sited behind the meter.
quotes: when generation to power large load is sited behind the meter, regulators should use cost-allocation principles that ensure no negative impacts to grid reliability or unfair cost shifts to other customers

letters.desc: By endorsing the call to prioritize ratepayer protections, the Michigan AG signals concern that cost allocation rules for large load interconnection must guard against shifting costs to existing customers.
quotes: The Attorney General also replies to express support for the request raised in comment by a group of several states' attorneys general and ratepayer advocates for FERC to "meaningfully prioritize ratepayer protections during this rulemaking process."

letters.desc: Microsoft supports fair, transparent cost allocation, accepting its share while wanting to avoid shifting costs to neighbors. It favors crediting mechanisms when up-front-funded upgrades deliver broad benefits, and sees joint studies as a way to lower transmission-upgrade costs.
quotes: Additionally, studying load and generation together potentially reduces the scale and cost of transmission upgrades by minimizing system impacts and the need for major backbone reinforcements.

In Microsoft’s view, the changes ripe for consideration are those that (i) focus on processes that will increase speed-to-market for new customers and new generation and (ii) reduce the cost and scope of network upgrades needed for interconnection.

Microsoft supports the work of utilities and regulators to make sure these costs are transparently calculated and assigned to it and the other customers who benefit from those capital investments. This work helps ensure that Microsoft’s neighbors and the local community do not pay for Microsoft’s share of the costs.

If the network upgrades (with costs paid for up-front by the interconnecting loads they are assigned to) are providing broad benefits to other system users—for example, if another industrial customer benefits from the same infrastructure —Microsoft believes it would be fair to use a crediting mechanism or other arrangement that would capture the reliability and economic value those network upgrades provide other electricity consumers.
One such approach may be similar to the crediting mechanisms used for interconnecting generator-only facilities.

letters.desc: The filer explicitly backs the ANOPR's goal that large load interconnection must not impose unfair cost shifts on other customers. They highlight state-level tariff efforts and data center agreements that produce customer savings as evidence that existing frameworks are working.
quotes: the MISO Transmission Owners strongly support the ANOPR's goals of interconnecting large loads in a timely and reliable manner that avoids unfair cost shifts.

letters.desc: The final rule must uphold cost causation principles and ensure that large load infrastructure costs are not shifted onto existing retail customers. It should include requirements to deter speculative projects, fairly allocate costs, and enhance transparency.
quotes: Standardized study procedures and a defined interconnection queue could reduce regulatory burden and uncertainty for large load customers, protect the safety and reliability of the transmission system, uphold cost causation principles, protect customers from stranded costs, and mitigate the risks of speculative projects that complicate state-level load forecasting and resource planning.

The Missouri PSC supports efficient and comprehensive study procedures of hybrid facilities, but emphasizes that hybrid facility arrangements must be structured to prevent harm to the local utility and other customers.
Other customers should not bear the costs of co-located generation that becomes unnecessary if, for example, data centers become more efficient over time.
The final rule should adopt strong requirements to deter speculative projects, fairly allocate costs and enhance transparency.

As Missouri and other state commissions confront issues of affordability in both wholesale and retail electricity rates, FERC must ensure that costs under its jurisdiction are allocated in a just and reasonable manner, and that other customers do not unjustly subsidize the energy needs of large load customers.

letters.desc: The Monitor contends data centers must pay for the full costs they impose, including generation, transmission upgrades, and reserve margin. Socializing those costs onto other customers is unjust, and requiring data centers to bring their own new generation is the mechanism to prevent it.
quotes: It is not unduly discriminatory to identify the class of large data centers and impose requirements on that class that match the impact of that class on all other customers.

It is not an overstatement to assert that the ongoing addition of large data center loads will put PJM competitive markets at risk unless there is a solution that requires large data center loads to pay for the costs that they would otherwise impose on other customers.

All of the currently identified options require PJM to plan the transmission system to meet large data center loads consistent with the RTEP and require all customers to pay an allocated share of the transmission upgrades required to serve large data center load additions.

letters.org: National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners
letters.desc: NARUC supports ensuring that interconnection costs, including transmission upgrades, are allocated fairly and do not impose undue burdens on existing retail ratepayers. Federal assertion of jurisdiction over a subset of retail customers would disrupt state rate-balancing across all customer classes.
quotes: If FERC were to assert jurisdiction over a service to a limited class of retail customers, it would interfere with the balancing performed by state regulators in retail rate cases, a determination that is solely a state decision, and which has significant rate impacts on all classes of customers.
the costs of large load interconnections, including necessary transmission upgrades and other infrastructure investments, may unfairly burden retail ratepayers if not properly allocated

letters.org: National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners
letters.desc: NARUC grounds the upgrade-cost allocation in the cost causation principle, assigning the full cost of upgrades to the large load customers that cause them.
quotes: Any proposed rule should specify that large load customers are responsible for 100% of the upgrade costs consistent with the cost causation principle.

letters.org: National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners
letters.desc: NARUC supports allocating large load interconnection and transmission costs to the large load customers themselves and preventing cost shifts to other ratepayers. It cites state tariffs using minimum demand charges, take-or-pay terms, exit fees, and collateral to achieve this, and warns federal preemption could impose negative cost consequences on other customers.
quotes: The abundance of recent state undertakings demonstrate that state commissions are in the best position to ensure rational and efficient interconnections of new large loads while protecting all customers (including residential, commercial and large manufacturing customers) from improper cost-shifts or unfair interconnection processes.

State commissions have the authority, regulatory tools, and unique expertise necessary to allocate transmission costs associated with large load interconnections directly to those end-use customers.  There is no regulatory gap.

NARUC also recognizes and supports the general conclusions of the Concentric Energy Advisors Whitepaper recently submitted into the record by WIRES, which highlights the potentially significant negative cost consequences to other retail customers of federal pre-emption of the large load interconnection process.

If FERC issues different federal rules for interconnection of data center loads, this may lead to increased costs or discriminatory procedures for other important end-use customers, such as Virginia manufacturers developing critical components

it remains unclear how cost allocation would work if some large loads have already paid for network upgrades through a federal interconnection process, making them exempt from other transmission costs at the retail level.  This could lead to costs being shifted to other retail ratepayers, while limiting the states’ ability to appropriately allocate costs and protect other customers.

this new large load tariff requires a minimum contract term of 14 years, a maximum ramp period of four years, minimum collateral requirements, and minimum demand charges based on contracted capacity.  All these protections will ensure that costs are not shifted to non-large load customers.
These terms ensure large loads pay their share even if they use less power than planned and prevent potential stranded asset costs from being passed to other retail ratepayers.

This sliding-scale approach provides appropriate incentives for customers to submit realistic and supportable demand forecasts and helps mitigate the risk of speculative or inflated requests that could lead to inefficient planning or unnecessary system investment.
no action in the ANOPR is necessary to enable state commission to cost-allocate transmission between end-use customers.

letters.org: National Association of State Utility Consumer Advocates
letters.desc: Protecting existing ratepayers from subsidizing large load interconnection is NASUCA's central concern. This means full cost assignment for network upgrades, strong financial readiness requirements to screen out speculative requests, and no crediting mechanisms that dilute cost causation.
quotes: NASUCA's primary interest in this proceeding is in ensuring that end-use customers' interests in reliable and affordable service are the lodestars that guide FERC's consideration of the ANOPR and potential reforms regarding the interconnection of large loads.
this rulemaking must include provisions that mitigate the risk of ratepayer subsidization of large load interconnection
making data centers responsible for 100% of the costs of network upgrades they are assigned
a crediting mechanism is directly contrary to this protective mechanism because it relieves large loads from a portion of the costs of network upgrades.
strong readiness and financial requirements to deter speculative large-load interconnection requests that can distort transmission planning and increase costs for consumers

letters.desc: Large load growth threatens grid reliability and consumer affordability. FERC must work with states to allocate costs using causation and beneficiary-pays principles, ensuring large-scale energy users pay their fair share rather than shifting costs to residential and small-business ratepayers.
quotes: total energy demand in the U.S. is expected to potentially increase 15% to 20% in the coming years and data centers' usage share of all electricity in the nation could more than double to almost 10% by 2030. This dramatic increase puts greater pressure on an overburdened and aging power grid and could significantly hamper reliability, raise costs for individual ratepayers, contribute to energy affordability challenges and cause serious cost-sharing concerns among residential users and small businesses.

How will FERC determine who is responsible for bearing the costs of increased power demand? FERC must work with states to create cost allocation methods that help ensure large-scale energy users are paying their fair share of costs using the 'cost causation' and 'beneficiary pays' principles while recognizing current jurisdiction on this issue.

letters.desc: National Grid argues that network upgrade costs should be allocated to beneficiaries, including both the triggering large load and other system users who gain benefit. Direct assignment of 100% of costs to the requesting customer would be unjust, create free-ridership for other users, and deprive utilities of a constitutionally required return.
quotes: It would not be just and reasonable to apply a 100% up-front Contributions in Aid of Construction ("CIAC") framework (as used for certain transmission facilities built to accommodate generator interconnections) to all transmission network upgrades triggered by large load interconnections.

Cost allocation approaches should take into account the principle that "beneficiaries pay" for the cost of network transmission investment, including both requesting customers and all transmission system users where both benefit.

Large loads interconnecting to the transmission system and generator interconnection customers occupy fundamentally different roles within the electric grid.  Generators function as wholesale electricity suppliers, feeding power into the system, while large loads are retail end-use consumers that draw power from the grid and pay delivery charges for their use of the electric system.

A rate design where a public utility is not permitted to earn a sufficient return on the significant capital investment necessary to provide interconnection service to large loads would violate Supreme Court standards and deprive public utilities of their property in violation of the Constitution.

letters.desc: NRECA backs full cost responsibility for large loads on cost-causation grounds, opposing any cost shift to existing customers. Incremental pricing for interconnection-related network upgrades is appropriate and sends efficient siting signals. Crediting rules should be case-by-case, not uniform.
