quotes: NRECA supports this principle as essential to keep rates affordable to other consumers and to protect them from cost shifting and stranded costs.
It stands to reason that the costs resulting from the direct access of large loads to the transmission grid should be borne by those who benefit from that access.

Interconnecting loads should be responsible for the costs of these network upgrades to ensure that other transmission customers do not bear stranded transmission costs for upgrades made to accommodate the interconnection of a large load that fails to materialize, does not take service in the anticipated volume or peak and off-peak patterns, or ceases operation.

utilities should have the flexibility to determine the appropriate financial security for such upgrades. The capital structure of most cooperatives, which, by design, runs lean on the debt/equity ratio, limits their ability to absorb the costs of the build-out associated with large loads in ways that do not unfairly burden other customers.
NRECA does not support a hard-and-fast rule on whether such a crediting mechanism is appropriate for large-load interconnections.

letters.org: Natural Resource Defense CouncilSustainable FERC ProjectClean Air Task Force ,Coalition for Affordable Utility Services and Energy Efficie ,EARTHJUSTICE ,ENVIRONMENTAL DEFENSE FUND ,MONTANA ENVIRONMENTAL INFORMATION CENTER ,Sierra Club ,Southern Environmental Law Center ,
letters.desc: The filers strongly support cost-causation discipline. Large loads are the sole or primary beneficiaries of the network upgrades they require, so they must bear 100% of those costs with no default crediting mechanism. The same principle bars allowing generators to suspend service to the broader market for a single customer, which shifts resource adequacy costs and blackout risk onto other ratepayers.
quotes: These recent price surges in PJM illustrate how the rapid and unregulated interconnection of new large loads can unjustly and unreasonably impose extreme costs and significant reliability risks on other consumers.

new large loads should be responsible for the costs they cause, and it would be unjust and unreasonable for the costs caused by new large loads to be shifted to existing consumers who did not cause those costs and who receive no, or trivial, benefits from the infrastructure developed to serve new large loads.

FERC should not adopt a default crediting mechanism to offset the costs of network upgrades required for large load interconnection. Again, because large loads are the sole or primary beneficiaries of the network upgrades required for their interconnection, it is appropriate for them to bear 100% of the costs of those upgrades.

PIOs do not believe that the Commission should adopt Principle 10. Many regions of the country are currently experiencing resource adequacy or reliability challenges. Generation that has been on the system and serving existing load should not be allowed to be essentially removed from the grid to serve a single customer.

the suspension of existing generation to serve new large loads is inconsistent with cost-causation principles and unjust and unreasonable because this practice shifts costs associated with maintaining resource adequacy onto other consumers, as well as increasing reliability risks for existing ratepayers.
It is unjust and unreasonable to force ordinary ratepayers to bear an increased risk of blackouts simply to facilitate new large loads buying up existing capacity.

letters.desc: NMPRC insists that generation and transmission costs associated with large loads must be evaluated and allocated through state planning and approval pathways. Federal approval without cost review would deprive the state of cost-allocation authority and risk shifting costs to retail customers.
quotes: the NMPRC seeks to ensure that the rulemaking adequately accounts for coordination with state regulatory processes and considers direct and indirect impacts to the NMPRC's authority over retail rates and cost recovery from retail customers in New Mexico.

states retain exclusive authority over retail sales, including retail rate design and the allocation of costs among retail customers. States alone determine which entities may sell power at retail and the rates, terms, and conditions of those retail sales.

FERC cannot require New Mexico ratepayers to finance new generation or infrastructure that has not gone through New Mexico's planning and approval requirements, whether initiated through the IRP process, certificate proceedings, or any of the other regulatory pathways the NMPRC uses to review and approve new resources.

if FERC assumes jurisdiction over approving new large loads, those interconnections could be approved without any proceeding to evaluate their associated costs, depriving the NMPRC of its ability to regulate interconnecting customers and determine how associated generation and transmission costs should be allocated to New Mexico ratepayers.

protection of state jurisdiction is essential to preventing retail customers from subsidizing large-load customers or bearing unplanned risks. FERC should ensure that any final rule respects the FPA's jurisdictional boundary and preserves New Mexico's sovereign authority to regulate retail service, resource decisions, and economic development consistent with state law and legislative priorities.

letters.desc: NREMC supports charging for ancillary services based on gross peak load without netting against co-located generation. The system must remain prepared to serve the full load at any time, and costs should reflect the full potential need for essential services.
quotes: NREMC agrees that utilities serving large loads should be responsible for ancillary services based on the gross peak load, without netting against any co-located generation. Even where generation is co-located, the system must still be prepared to serve the full load at any time, maintaining the ability to provide black start, regulation, reactive power, and other essential services.
Co-location does not reduce the system's obligations or the risk the load imposes, and charges for ancillary services should reflect the full potential need to deploy these capabilities.

letters.desc: NRG strongly backs assigning 100 percent of network upgrade costs to the interconnecting load and criticizes state minimum-commitment provisions as disconnected from actual cost causation. Open seasons would also achieve direct cost allocation, and any surplus would reduce costs for existing customers.
quotes: NRG strongly supports the principles set forth in the ANOPR but proposes several discrete modifications to ensure that the final rule successfully implements those principles.

NRG strongly supports the Secretary's proposed eighth principle for large load interconnection: that "load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades that they are assigned through the interconnection studies."

many state-regulated utilities seek a "revenue guarantee" based on embedded cost rates multiplied by the MW-demand of the data center for some length of time.  Sometimes called "minimum commitments," this provision has been advertised as a policy approach that causes data centers to pay their fair share of grid costs, which may suggest alignment with the eighth principle announced in the ANOPR, but this is not an accurate understanding of the details of the "revenue guarantee" or "minimum commitments" provisions which have so far been adopted by state commissions.

the transmission and distribution revenues guaranteed by a large load addition customer could be substantially more or substantially less the revenue requirement of the transmission and distribution investments that would not have been needed but for that customers' large load addition.
fail[s] to send a price signal for large load additions to locate in locations where the required transmission . . . investments for the large load would be lower.

This open season or auction achieves a direct cost allocation of both interconnection and network upgrade costs, preventing cost shifts to other customers.  Surplus revenue from the open season should be applied against the transmission owner's transmission revenue requirement, reducing costs for all other customers.

letters.org: Office of the Ohio Consumers' Counsel
letters.desc: OCC insists that large loads bear 100% of interconnection and upgrade costs. Crediting mechanisms and regional cost allocation must not be used for facilities built primarily to serve private large loads, and any cost shift requires demonstrated net public benefit. This aligns with ICC I and ICC II cost causation precedent.
quotes: this proposal presents substantial risks to residential consumers, who could bear higher costs and diminished oversight as transmission policy shifts to accommodate extraordinary private demand growth from large industrial and data center loads.
such "credits" frequently evolve into generalized cost socialization—resulting in rate impacts borne by retail residential customers who do not benefit from the facilities being built.
Prohibit the use of transmission credits, rate-based recovery, or regional cost allocation mechanisms for interstate transmission facilities built primarily to serve large private loads

Ensure that transmission cost recovery aligns with current cost causation and cost allocation principles developed in Illinois Commerce Commission v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 476 (7th Cir. 2009) (ICC I) ("FERC is not authorized to approve a pricing scheme that requires a group of utilities to pay for facilities from which its members derive no benefits, or benefits that are trivial in relation to the costs sought to be shifted to its members.")

Annual reporting on the consumer cost impacts of large-load interconnections, associated transmission expansions, and the impact on electricity and capacity markets rates for consumers other than large loads.
The Commission should affirm that no interconnection right or transmission upgrade will be granted unless the applicant bears 100% of the costs of interconnection-related costs.
The cost of obtaining replacement capacity should not be borne by existing consumers who have relied on and been paying for the suspension resources for many years.
Consumers should not bear the financial or reliability burdens of speculative industrial growth.

letters.desc: Ohio FEA requires that new data center loads and hybrid facilities be responsible for 100% of network upgrades and a fair share of both new and existing transmission and ancillary system costs they will use and benefit from, ensuring costs do not shift to other customers.
quotes: new data center loads should not impose costs on other customers or customer classes
large load and hybrid facilities (new load and generation in proximity) should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades resulting from their interconnection studies

Newly interconnecting large loads must be allocated a fair and equitable share of the costs related to the transmission system that they will utilize and benefit from, both new and existing, as well as the grid ancillary systems upon which they will rely.

letters.desc: Large load interconnection customers should bear 100% of transmission upgrades they trigger and pay for transmission service based on actual withdrawal and injection rights requested, not gross load. This directly applies cost causation and prevents cross-subsidization across ratepayers.
quotes: costs should be allocated to those who cause them and benefit from the resulting services. This is essential for ensuring just and reasonable rates
load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades that they are assigned through the interconnection studies. This aligns directly with the cost causation principle.
If these costs are not assigned to the interconnection customer, they are socialized across ratepayers. Such cross-subsidization is inequitable and economically inefficient

letters.desc: Oracle commits to funding all infrastructure costs for its data centers and signing the Ratepayer Protection Pledge to protect consumers from energy price increases. quotes: a system should be established to provide credit back for study deposits, but perhaps through transmission credits.

letters.desc: The filer argues that flexible loads raise revenue on existing wires without new construction and, when exposed to real-time prices, shift away from peaks and cut uplift charges, lowering costs for all consumers.
quotes: In instances where utilities do not have to build more transmission to connect flexible loads, they can increase revenue on the same infrastructure, wires, and substations. Prior to TDSP rate adjustments, this increased revenue can, in turn, help pay for additional transmission projects assuming guidelines have been developed outlining what transmission charges apply to these loads when they are co-located, at the same POI.

When these loads are exposed to real-time prices and congestion signals, they shift consumption away from peak periods using a variety of market-based tools, reducing uplift charges and lessening the need for emergency procurement.

letters.desc: VPPs can lower capacity procurement needs and defer or avoid costly network upgrades. Pew argues this aligns with DOE's cost-minimization objectives for large load interconnection.
quotes: VPPs have the potential to lower capacity procurement needs and defer or avoid costly network upgrades associated with interconnecting large loads, while supporting distributed energy systems that provide consumers savings.

letters.desc: Pew frames VPP inclusion as a tool to keep interconnection affordable for existing customers. VPPs can offset capacity and network upgrade costs that large load additions would otherwise impose, and their faster deployment reduces the period during which supply-demand imbalances inflate prices.
quotes: Adopting rules that allow integrated, expedited study of large loads that contract with VPPs will facilitate speed-to-power for large load customers while keeping transmission and energy affordable for existing customers.
VPPs are critically positioned to allow the timely interconnection of large loads while protecting existing customers from adverse impacts and allowing for additional benefits.

Pew urges the Commission to draft its rules in such a way that unlocks the multiple benefits that VPPs can provide both to existing transmission customers and large load customers seeking to interconnect while keeping electricity rates affordable and maintaining grid reliability.

letters.desc: TBA supports cost allocation tied to actual system impacts: flexible loads that avoid peak demand should not bear peak-driven upgrade or capacity costs. Inaccurate modeling inflates cost assignments, biases the market toward inflexible loads, and raises costs for consumers. Non-firm service election should reduce both interconnection and capacity requirements.
quotes: When tariffs treat all loads as inflexible peak contributors, they distort competition, raise barriers to entry, and suppress innovation in flexible industrial technologies.
Current modeling practices often inaccurately assume flexible loads will operate inflexibly, resulting in assignment of unnecessary network upgrade costs, resource requirements and reserve margin.
Such mis-modeling functions as a regulatory barrier to competition, encouraging only high-load factor and low-flexibility loads, resulting in an under-utilized grid and higher costs for consumers.

Flexible loads that select non-firm service and can avoid peak loads should receive reduced interconnection and transmission upgrade requirements, and should avoid all network resource and resource adequacy/capacity requirements.
Cost allocation should reflect the principle that customers pay the costs they impose on the system, minus any benefits they provide.

letters.desc: TBA argues that non-firm loads do not cause peak-driven infrastructure needs and must not be allocated upgrade costs based on hours when they are contractually barred from taking service. This directly addresses state commission concerns about cost shifts to retail customers.
quotes: the absence of a clear, Commission‑directed, non‑firm service option risks perpetuating unreasonable and inefficient outcomes, including the misallocation of upgrade costs to loads that do not contribute to system peaks
TBA urges the Commission to require every jurisdictional transmission provider to offer at least one non‑firm network transmission service option tailored to large flexible loads
customers with non-firm withdrawal rights do not impose the same peak-driven infrastructure needs as firm network integration transmission service ("NITS") customers
the Commission should require that non-firm loads not be assigned costs for upgrades based on hours in which they are contractually barred from taking service

letters.desc: Tract consistently argues that all financial requirements, deposits, security amounts, and upgrade cost assignments must follow cost-causation principles and align with the generator interconnection precedent. Over-sized charges will deter investment in data center development.
quotes: Tract agrees with adopting standardized study deposits, readiness requirements, and withdrawal penalties, provided that they are consistent with the Commission's cost-causation principles.

Adopting deposits or penalties that are not sized to reflect a project's impact on the system will unnecessarily and economically deter data center development, threatening the ability to achieve the Administration's dual goals of energy dominance and winning the AI race.

The Commission should establish a standardized methodology, whether by requiring fixed deposit amounts based on load size, by kWh, or through another metric, whereby customers can reasonably calculate anticipated charges and plan their investments accordingly.

Tract appreciates the need to provide financial security for load interconnection requests, but believes financial security requirements should be clear, predictable, in line with cost-causation, and tied to project progress.

Consistent with the Commission's cost-causation principles, financial security should only be required for actual incremental costs caused by the large load customer, and should not provide a windfall to transmission providers in the event of default.

Tract recommends the Commission require large load interconnection customers to only post financial security as they approach key project milestones (i.e., to support detailed design, permitting and right-of-way acquisition, procurement, pad acceptance, construction and energization), rather than up front as a lump sum because this places an unnecessary financial burden on the large load interconnection customer and creates incremental impediments to development.

To the extent any network upgrades are assigned through interconnection studies to load or hybrid facilities, such costs should be offset through a crediting mechanism based on the actual usage of those upgrades by other networked customers.

letters.desc: The central theme of the filing is that other transmission customers must not bear costs caused by large load interconnections. TAPS supports 100% upfront cost responsibility, tailored crediting that prevents stranded costs, and a Commission directive requiring retail stranded-cost protections to flow through to wholesale transmission rates.
quotes: the Commission must be proactive in addressing the huge impact that the interconnections of Qualifying Large Loads have on Commission-jurisdictional services to protect transmission customers—and, ultimately, other end-use individual and business ratepayers—from paying costs they did not cause.

a major concern with Qualifying Loads interconnections is that they may complete the interconnection process and cause major transmission upgrades to be constructed, but then fail to either attain, or maintain over a long period of time, the level of demand for which the interconnection request was studied.

TAPS supports holding Qualifying Large Load and Hybrid Facilities responsible for 100% of the network upgrades that they are assigned. Principle 8 is key to addressing one of the most important challenges raised by large data centers and other similar loads: that, if rolled into wholesale transmission rates, the substantial costs of transmission upgrades needed to serve these unique loads gets borne by other customers
the Commission cannot achieve this goal by merely copying the existing crediting mechanisms used for different purposes in the different context of generator interconnections.
any crediting mechanism must account for the unique risks and characteristics of large data center loads to protect other customers.

the Commission should find that it is unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory for a public utility to charge rates that fail to reflect the impact of ratepayer protections imposed by retail arrangements with Qualifying Large Loads.

the Commission should ensure that other customers are protected from harm resulting from large data center load interconnections already being studied, as well as earlier data center-driven network upgrades that are subject to ratepayer protection provisions by contract or retail tariff.

letters.desc: TAPS consistently frames FERC action as necessary to prevent large load-driven stranded costs and cost shifting from falling on other wholesale and retail transmission customers. A uniform federal rule is more effective and efficient than piecemeal state or contract-by-contract arrangements.
quotes: action by this Commission is required to address the clear and direct impact that large load interconnections have on transmission rates within the Commission's exclusive jurisdiction.

The Commission is statutorily obligated to ensure just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory transmission rates; only the Commission can protect other wholesale transmission customers from the risks of significant large load-driven cost shifting and stranded costs that would otherwise occur through Commission-jurisdictional rates.

If that large load fails to achieve and sustain demand at the level for which these network upgrades were built, the costs of the upgrades will be allocated based on load ratio shares that do not reflect the addition of a large load (whose demand projections triggered the upgrades) to the peak load of the LSE serving that large load.

Holding large loads responsible for the costs of network upgrades they cause, as contemplated in the ANOPR, is the most protective of other wholesale transmission customers paying Commission-jurisdictional rates.
Consistent large load cost responsibility requirements would also allow the Commission to ensure just and reasonable rates in a manner that is quick and efficient compared to a piecemeal approach.

At minimum, the Commission must ensure that the results of protective measures adopted at the retail level (e.g., minimum demand charges, minimum contract terms, exit fees, etc.) are properly reflected in transmission rates.

Under that mechanism, the large load would pay the upfront cost of any network upgrades, but it would have the opportunity to be credited back that full amount, so long as its transmission usage over time is sufficient to cover the costs.

This ensures that the large load pays the higher of either incremental costs or rolled-in transmission rates, mitigating the stranded cost risks to other wholesale customers if the large load fails to maintain a level of demand sufficient to justify the cost of the network upgrades caused by the large load.

letters.desc: The Coalition argues storage-backed load flexibility during peak events can reduce or eliminate the need for costly, multi-year network upgrades.
quotes: Enabling large loads to avoid drawing from the grid by maintaining dispatchable energy during peak demand events—when transmission constraints are most salient—can dramatically reduce or eliminate the need for network upgrades that would otherwise require years of study and construction (as well as sizeable costs) to accommodate.

letters.desc: UCS strongly supports assigning 100 percent of identified network upgrade costs to the large loads that cause them. The filing documents that over $4 billion in connection costs were added to ratebases in 2024 across seven states, and explains how the current regulatory gap allows data center costs to be socialized across all retail customers while revenues from those customers are credited only to the largest customer class.
quotes: we recommend that the Commission convene a workgroup of technical experts to develop such requirements. These requirements should be responsive to available technical capability and should prioritize reliability while avoiding excessive costs to developers and consumers.
Costs for transmission connections and network extensions required by new large loads have already added over $4 billion to the ratebase of utilities in 2024 from construction in just seven states.
The existing rules and practices allow the worst outcome: the rapidly rising costs for data centers' needs are spread across all the utilities' customers.

Under existing practices the revenues from new large load customers are recognized for the largest customer class, but the costs caused by those customers are allocated to all customers. This is not the application of the 'Bonbright' cost-causation principle that is so often cited in utility cost allocation debates.

this proposed Principle of assigning costs for all upgrades identified in the interconnection studies for large loads will address a regulatory gap and correctly apply the widely cited principle of cost causation to significant costs presently misallocated to all consumers.

letters.desc: The Congress members argue that current allocation practices push data center transmission upgrade costs onto existing ratepayers, raising utility bills. They ask FERC to add explicit safeguards preventing large load customers from shifting interconnection or upgrade costs to existing customers.
quotes: Rate payers in markets with data centers have been subject to higher utility bills as the costs of transmission upgrades and expansions are distributed based on current allocation practices.
Safeguards to prevent large load customers from shifting interconnection or transmission upgrade costs onto existing rate payers.

letters.desc: The filer argues that any large-load interconnection rule must prevent cost-shifting onto residential ratepayers. Data centers and other large loads should bear their own energy costs, and FERC should treat consumer affordability as the primary measure of a rule's success.
quotes: Working families and seniors living on fixed incomes shouldn't be subsidizing the energy costs of data centers and other large load customers.
As we advance new energy intensive projects, we must ensure that consumer prices and the interests of the American taxpayer guide any new rules or regulatory changes.
As FERC considers regulatory action, I urge the Commission to prioritize policies that result in lower energy costs for consumers.
Should FERC pursue ambiguity in any rule to meet an arbitrarily condensed timeline, it will undermine an opportunity to lower energy costs for consumers.

If FERC and DoE are serious about implementing a creative rule that will both lower costs for consumers and recognize the growing need for data centers and energy heavy projects, they must prioritize affordability and take the time necessary to get the policy right so that it lowers costs for consumers.

letters.desc: The Senator supports ensuring data centers bear their own grid infrastructure costs rather than passing them to Georgia families. He asks FERC to assess whether tech company pledges to pay their own way are credible and enforceable, and flags the risk that capital costs from new generation get socialized to residential customers.
quotes: My office is investigating AI data centers' impact on rising power bills in Georgia and nationwide.
Without proper safeguards, higher prices and capital costs from increased energy generation could be passed onto Georgia families.

Prominent technology companies have made public commitments to "pay their own way" when it comes to data center power usage and infrastructure costs. Does FERC assess these to be credible and/or enforceable commitments?

letters.org: Utility Intervention Unit, New York State Department of Stat
letters.desc: The UIU strongly supports the beneficiary-pays principle and opposes any rule that socializes large-load upgrade costs to existing ratepayers. Shared-benefit allocations are acceptable only when benefits are technically and rigorously demonstrable.
quotes: Data centers often require substantial grid upgrades, and unless carefully managed, these costs risk being unfairly shifted to residential and small business ratepayers who do not directly benefit.

Protecting consumers means ensuring that developers bear the costs of infrastructure driven by their own demand (ignoring co-located generation), that planning processes remain open to public scrutiny, and that regional coordination prevents unintended reliability or cost consequences.

Each large load project's cost responsibility must reflect the incremental cost of required local and network upgrades, ensuring that large load developers fund the infrastructure needed to support their own demand.
Costs unsupported by quantifiable benefits must not be socialized to general transmission customers.
UIU urges the Commission to protect consumers from bearing adverse impacts from large load integration, particularly from energy-intensive developments like data centers.

letters.desc: Vantage fully supports assigning large loads the full cost of network upgrades their interconnection causes, consistent with cost causation principles. Vantage also asks for a transmission rate crediting mechanism so that data center customers are not charged both the full upgrade cost and the system average embedded transmission cost.
quotes: Vantage emphasizes that the specific principles and reforms concerning (1) hybrid interconnecting data center facilities supported in whole or in part by dedicated generating facilities (Principles 3 and 5), (2) expedited interconnection study procedures (Principle 7), (3) cost allocation for interconnection-related network upgrades (Principle 8), and (4) a fair and structured transition that respects existing rights (Principle 13) are of greatest importance.

The recommendation of Proposed ANOPR Principle 8 that large loads should be fully responsible for assigned network upgrades attributable to their interconnection accords fully with Vantage's commitment to absorb the full cost of upgrades required by its projects.

a transmission rate crediting mechanism is appropriate to ensure full compliance with the Commission's 'higher of' transmission pricing principle by ensuring that the data center customer is not allocated the full cost of network upgrades caused by its interconnection plus the system average embedded cost of transmission.

letters.desc: VEIR supports cost-allocation frameworks that reflect savings from advanced conductors, including crediting avoided upgrades and allowing self-build options that lower costs for large load developers.
quotes: VEIR invites FERC to consider in the ANOPR stage: (a) whether study cost-allocation frameworks should recognize reduced ROW and environmental impact associated with innovative cable technology; (b) whether pilot or demonstration status of such technologies merits expedited interconnection treatment; and (c) how manufacturing scale-up of such systems may reduce long-lead supply-chain delays that currently hamper large-load attachments.

VEIR is encouraged by the principles outlined in the ANOPR and particularly supports Principles 8 and 9, which highlight the value of allowing large load developers to build or fund their own network upgrades. We believe this flexibility can accelerate deployment and create space for innovative technical approaches to interconnection and co-location of load and generation.
Ensure cost-allocation frameworks acknowledge when interconnection upgrades are mitigated or avoided entirely by advanced conductors while allowing crediting for non-traditional upgrade paths.

Allow large loads (or load developers) to own or build portions of the interconnection infrastructure (including superconducting feeders) under engineer-and-construct options equal to those available to generators. This is consistent with DOE's principle allowing self-build.

letters.desc: Verrus supports cost allocation that reflects what flexible loads actually cause. Because flexible loads can avoid or defer network upgrades through curtailment commitments, their upgrade assignments and credit requirements should be reduced accordingly.
quotes: Today, the benefits of load flexibility are neither accounted for nor compensated. As a result, flexible resources are discouraged from the market and cannot practically be used to accelerate interconnection times or to protect consumers from the costs of load growth.

Flexible loads that meet this definition should also be allowed to nominate operational flexibility commitments in the study process that allow the Transmission Provider to avoid, reduce, or defer network upgrades, thereby accelerating interconnection and reducing system costs.

The Commission should require transmission providers to explicitly model flexible-load curtailment potential in their base-case and sensitivity analyses so that flexibility is valued in interconnection studies with respect to network upgrades, and in the studies that underlie local and regional transmission planning.

Credit assurance should protect ratepayers from stranded-cost risk—not serve as a barrier to participation. Today, many utilities require deposits equal to multiple years of transmission revenue or theoretical upgrade costs regardless of a project's actual risk profile or contribution to bulk system upgrades. Such rules privilege only the largest incumbents and exclude technically capable but less capitalized entrants.

Credit requirements should scale with the actual infrastructure spend required to interconnect the large load. As in the generator interconnection process, credit requirements should secure actual interconnection costs, but only during the period of construction when ratepayers are exposed to those costs.

letters.desc: Verrus strongly opposes assigning full network upgrade costs to loads that commit to curtailment and therefore do not cause the need for the upgrade. The filing argues that flexible loads currently cross-subsidize inflexible ones and calls on FERC to ensure any tariff structure lets flexible loads avoid upgrade cost assignment through curtailment commitments.
quotes: the current framework forces flexible loads to cross-subsidize inflexible ones, requiring customers who can operationally avoid the need for network upgrades to pay for infrastructure that is only necessary for their inflexible peers.

Verrus strongly opposes proposals that would assign network upgrade costs directly to a large load customer if that customer has made commitments to exercise operational flexibility to avoid triggering the upgrade.
Assigning the full cost of a network upgrade to a flexible load that has committed to curtail—and thus does not cause the need for the upgrade—would be unjust and unreasonable.

It could create a separate "Flexible Large Load" interconnection class with distinct processes and transmission service cost structures, or establish separate classes of transmission service (e.g., conditional firm service) that large loads can select.

letters.desc: Vistra argues that cost causation principles must govern all network upgrade cost allocation and that transmission service charges for co-located facilities should reflect actual net load rather than gross load. Without standardized rules, existing customers risk shouldering costs caused by new loads.
quotes: The lack of rates, terms, and conditions for transmission-level load interconnection has created a vacuum in which utilities are exercising unfettered discretion to determine, among other things, the process by which large loads interconnecting to the transmission system are studied, how to allocate the costs incurred to facilitate those load interconnections, and whether to allow large loads to interconnect to the transmission system at all.

the studies involving the interconnection of new loads must focus on studying the impacts to the transmission system.  As noted above, states retain jurisdiction over generation facilities.  With that in mind, and consistent with the Commission's jurisdiction over the transmission system -- and interconnections to it -- load interconnection studies must be focused on identifying the transmission system upgrades needed to facilitate the interconnection and allocating the costs of those upgrades in a manner consistent with the Commission's cost causation principles.

the current lack of standardized study deposits, readiness requirements, and withdrawal penalties increases the prevalence of speculative projects and the related risk that ratepayers will be saddled with costs incurred due to projects that never materialize.

co-location arrangements involving new generators will require new tariff language to effectuate the coordinated and expedited study of new load co-located with new generation.  The Commission should prioritize doing so as soon as possible because it 'will allow for efficient siting of loads and generating facilities and thereby minimize the need for costly network upgrades.'
in keeping with the cost causation principle, transmission service charges should be based on actual use of the transmission system, as measured by the facility's net load.

letters.desc: Vistra endorses participant funding without crediting as the cleanest approach to cost causation, ensuring large loads bear 100% of the network upgrade costs they cause and other ratepayers are held harmless. It opposes embedded-cost rollover because it creates cost-shift risk if a large load fails to materialize.
quotes: Cost causation principles require that the parties to such an arrangement fund any necessary network upgrades, and the transmission service that facilitates these arrangements be determined by actual use of the transmission system based on their net load.
transmission providers should serve, and charge, co-located facilities based on their actual use of the transmission system, i.e., based on their net—not gross—injections and withdrawals.

Providing transmission service to co-located facilities based on their actual use of the transmission system will incentivize more new large loads to interconnect via co-location, which is undoubtedly the large load interconnection model most likely to fulfill speed-to-power needs while minimizing strain on the grid.

The third option, to contrast, creates a significant risk of cost shifts to other customers if a large load customer fails to materialize, consumes less energy than intended, or ceases operation sooner than anticipated.

Participant funding also furthers speed to power by providing cost certainty that can be built into a large load customer's commercial negotiations, whereas a crediting approach could entail more uncertainty and necessitate a risk premium in commercial arrangements.

letters.desc: Off-site distributed solutions and bring-your-own-capacity (BYOC) programs significantly reduce consumer costs and place downward pressure on rates. Research quantifies that BYOC can internalize $326 million in capacity costs per GW while accelerating data center interconnection timelines.
quotes: distributed solutions significantly mitigate system costs borne by consumers, placing downward pressure on rates in a load growth environment
BYOC internalizes $326 million in capacity costs per GW, with the data center procuring accredited resources directly and offering them into the market to increase supply.

letters.desc: The filer argues that ATTs lower congestion costs, improve investment efficiency, and protect ratepayers. It cites Basin Electric's DLR deployment recovering capital costs in 38 days and saving over $20 million in 2024, and contends that reporting requirements on GETs potential are essential to ensuring just and reasonable rates.
quotes: requiring ATTs to be evaluated in interconnection processes is valuable, it is not sufficient to enable large load interconnection at the fastest reasonable pace and lowest possible cost.

The time has come and gone for voluntary or incentivized consideration of GETs. It is well documented that use of GETs delivers cost reductions and cost avoidance to the benefit of consumers nationwide. Despite this, relatively few projects have been implemented.

The transparency envisioned by these reporting requirements is also critical to ensuring just and reasonable rates by identifying opportunities to maximize the use of our existing grid, to the benefit of ratepayers across the country, and to ensure our investments in new transmission are efficient and cost effective—key components of just and reasonable rates.

We urge the Commission to act, through a policy statement or order directing reports, to encourage transmission owners and RTOs to develop processes focused on improving grid efficiency. These processes could unlock latent grid capacity in the timescales needed to win the AI race–the next two to three years—as well as to address the growing affordability crisis.

The WATT Coalition has proposed a federal shared savings incentive that allows transmission owners to profit based on a portion of the congestion cost savings from GETs deployments. This directly links utility profits to consumer benefits and operational efficiency.

ATTs can deliver meaningful increases in transmission capacity to facilitate the interconnection of large load in less than three years. While recent deployments by PG&E, Georgia Power and others validate this potential, utility adoption remains limited.

letters.desc: WIRES asks the Commission to preserve transmission owners' opportunity to recover costs and earn a reasonable return on the upgrades and expansions needed to interconnect large loads. It argues the existing rolled-in rates and transmission pricing policy should apply, with large load customers paying the full cost of service consistent with longstanding precedent and retail regulator interests.
quotes: Finally, WIRES also seeks clarification that any further action taken in this proceeding will protect utilities’ ability to build the transmission upgrades and expansions needed to interconnect large loads and preserve their opportunity to earn a return on those investments.
The Commission has a long-standing policy in favor of rolled-in rates for integrated systems.

transmission owners should be able to recover the costs of serving all loads and the manner in which that is done should respect Commission precedent and consider the interests of retail regulators in setting retail rates.

the Commission should require that its overall existing transmission service pricing policy is applicable to new large loads.  That is, as they do today, such load customers should pay for the cost of transmission service with such costs reflecting the upgrades and expansions necessary to interconnect and serve such large load customers, over both the short and long term.

The Commission must ensure that transmission owners can timely recover their costs and investment and earn a reasonable rate of return for the risks and costs associated with their development, ownership, and operation of the transmission upgrades and expansions needed to achieve the Administration’s goal of expeditiously interconnecting large loads.

letters.desc: ATC supports cost-causation principles and penalties for unauthorized usage but argues that network upgrades serving the shared grid should be socialized. ATC recommends directly assigning only the identifiable, exclusive-use facilities and non-conforming-behavior equipment costs.
quotes: If hybrid facilities are not process-matched and the load exceeds studied levels, the transmission system becomes the 'backstop,' and other customers subsidize that excess use through shared costs and reliability impacts.

ATC strongly supports principles that uphold cost responsibility and maintain reliability, including proposed penalties for unauthorized injections or withdrawals.  However, any implementation plan must avoid unintended cost shifts and ensure transparency for transmission customers.
ATC maintains that such costs should be socialized because these network upgrades ultimately benefit all customers.
ATC recommends that the Commission narrowly tailor direct assignment of interconnection facility costs to those that can be directly attributed to and likely exclusively used by the new load.

the Commission should consider requiring new loads to bear 100% of the costs for facilities necessitated by their characteristics that do not conform with planning and interconnection criteria addressing behavior such as oscillation, ramp, and low-voltage ride-through.

letters.desc: Bloom supports assigning 100% of upgrade costs tied to generator injections to hybrid facility generators, consistent with existing policy. However, it opposes any rule denying cash-equivalent refunds, calling such a rule unduly discriminatory and a deterrent to needed generation.
quotes: Properly structured hybrid facility interconnection procedures will incentivize data centers to deploy on-site generation that meets their peak loads, thereby easing resource adequacy concerns while protecting existing customers from costs.

Like the ANOPR, Brattle finds that an integrated interconnection study approach for new load and new generation based on requested firm withdrawals and injections can significantly reduce the need for transmission upgrades, potentially avoiding billions in transmission expansion costs.

the proposal for hybrid facility generators to be responsible for 100% of identified Network Upgrades associated with their requested injections but potentially without cash equivalent refunds should be rejected.  There is no reason to treat cash equivalent refunds for such Network Upgrades differently from other generators that are subject to the Commission's pro forma rules or RTO rules.
Treating a hybrid facility generator differently than other generation subject to FERC jurisdiction would be unduly discriminatory.
Given these benefits, the Commission should decline to adopt rules that could dissuade much needed generation to serve large load by creating unduly discriminatory cash equivalent refund rules.

letters.desc: The CPUC supports cost allocation principles commensurate with benefits and opposes any federal rule that would bypass state-level decisions on upgrade cost recovery, crediting periods, and rate design. Reimbursement periods for load customers should be longer than the five years used for generators.
quotes: The CPUC supports ratepayer protections and efforts to mitigate risks associated with stranded or mis-sized transmission assets.

For any cost offsets (i.e., reimbursements to large load customers) for transmission network upgrades, it is imperative that they occur over a period sufficient to ensure that risks to other ratepayers associated with the failure of generation to timely materialize, and costs borne while load ramps up, are fully mitigated.

the five years over which payback to generators occurs is likely too short a period to ensure that load will develop and be sustained.  Any reimbursement to load customers for their upfront investment in load energization upgrade costs would likely need to occur over longer than five years to ensure protection of other ratepayers.

letters.desc: DEC accepts that large loads should bear their assigned upgrade costs, but argues that facilities demonstrating verifiable curtailment or on-site generation should qualify for phased or partial cost responsibility. It also supports extending option-to-build rights so developers can self-finance approved upgrades.
quotes: Developers face multi-year queues, inconsistent study processes, and unclear cost responsibilities that slow deployment and create uncertainty.

Current procedures force developers to complete separate studies for generation and load, even when they are part of a single co-located facility. This duplication increases costs, creates conflicting assumptions, and slows project development.

The Commission should extend the "option-to-build" authority, currently available to generator interconnection customers to qualifying large-load and hybrid facilities, subject to Commission oversight and cost-crediting provisions.

The Commission should affirm DOE's principle that large loads and hybrid facilities remain responsible for their assigned upgrade costs but clarify that those demonstrating verifiable curtailment or on-site generation may qualify for phased or partial cost responsibility.
Aligning cost responsibility with actual system impact ensures fair treatment, promotes investment in flexible technologies, and encourages efficient infrastructure development.

letters.org: Industrial Energy Consumers of America et al.
letters.desc: The filers strongly support cost-causation principles but oppose applying a blanket 100% upgrade cost mandate to all new loads. They argue that speed-driven, large-scale entrants like data centers should bear full 'but for' upgrade costs, while manufacturers with methodical growth plans should continue under the existing beneficiary-pays framework. Net billing for behind-the-meter generation must also be preserved.
quotes: Cost impacts cannot be measured solely in terms of the direct cost of infrastructure. Speed-to-market demands, volatility in load forecasts, and the potential for stranded assets must also be considered in evaluating cost responsibility.

mandating 100% cost responsibility for all network upgrades triggered by a new large load interconnection would bring an unjust and unreasonable result in some cases, particularly where growth is methodical, planned, and fits within the existing framework, and where existing customers in the impacted utility zone are generally allocated costs of new network upgrades that benefit them.
Requiring All New Loads, Including Manufacturers, to Be Responsible for 100% of Network Upgrades They Are Assigned, Is Contrary to Longstanding Cost Causation Principles.
Customers with behind-the-meter generation should be billed on a net basis (accounting for their net demand requirements) and not on a gross load basis.
the Commission should also evaluate the potential refinements as to how the cost causation and beneficiary pays principles are applied in the context of different large load interconnection requests.

letters.org: New York Transmission OwnersCentral Hudson Gas & Electric CorporationNew York Power Authority ,New York State Electric & Gas Corp. and Rochester Gas and El ,Niagara Mohawk d/b/a/ National Grid ,Consolidated Edison Company of New York, Inc. and Orange and ,Long Island Power Authority ,
letters.desc: The NYTOs support cost frameworks that ensure transmission owners recover prudently incurred costs plus a regulated return, and that cost-causer customers bear the economic weight of dedicated facilities. They oppose any federal rule presuming all upgrade costs must be directly assigned to the interconnecting customer, which would conflict with state retail ratemaking and could undermine transmission owner financial capacity.
quotes: customers that drive new costs should bear the economic weight of the facilities dedicated to their use; Transmission Owners should have the right to recover their costs plus a regulated return when they construct, own, and operate assets upon which the system relies; and federal actions should not upend established allocation frameworks or compel Transmission Owners to operate facilities without full cost-of-service recovery, including an authorized return.

A nationwide rule that presumes all upgrade costs must be directly assigned to the interconnecting load customer would not account for these distinctions and could conflict with existing state-jurisdictional approaches to resource adequacy, retail ratemaking, and customer protection.

Option-to-build authority is appropriate only for facilities used exclusively by the requesting customer and only where: (1) the facilities are not used or relied upon for network transmission service; (2) the customer assumes full lifecycle responsibility and NERC obligations if the asset qualifies as a BES facility; (3) the Transmission Owner retains authority over system protection, interconnection criteria, switching, and operational coordination at the point of interconnection; and (4) no ongoing operation and maintenance, modeling, or retrofit obligations shift to the Transmission Owner absent Section 205 cost of service recovery.

letters.desc: WIRES argues that a sole direct-assignment policy undermines cost equity because large loads would eventually contribute less to transmission cost recovery than if charged standard NITS rates. The filing urges careful review of any policy that could shift billions in costs to residential and other retail customers, while declining to endorse a specific alternative framework.
quotes: The Whitepaper sets forth an analysis of the ANOPR's proposal to allocate 100 percent of network upgrade costs to large load customers and illustrates the potential for unintended cost shifts to retail customers under certain implementation scenarios.
directly assigning network upgrade costs to large load customers can lead to significant transmission cost shifts away from large load customers onto other retail customers.

Our core finding is that direct assignment of network upgrade costs, with accompanying excusal from paying NITS charges, results in significant transmission cost shifts away from the large load customers and onto other customers.
over time, these cost shifts could amount to $33-47 billion in present value terms for just the volume of large loads expected to be developed in PJM from 2025-2030.

if the Commission were to implement in PJM a sole direct assignment policy for network upgrades associated with large loads interconnecting in the 2025-2030 period, the average PJM customer could experience an approximately 8-11 percent increase in the transmission portion of their retail electricity bill, or about $23-33 more per year in 2026 dollars.

it shows that when large loads pay only for their required network upgrades and do not contribute to the embedded system costs or the future costs required to maintain system reliability for all customers, including themselves, those costs are shifted onto other customers.

special attention should be given to data that highlights potential unintended consequences that could flow from certain rate structures or cost allocation methodologies which may adversely impact customer affordability.
This approach creates a problematic cost shift from an equity and policy standpoint. Furthermore, such rate treatment ignores the reality that the transmission system is an evolving investment.

letters.org: Wisconsin Electric Power CompanyWisconsin Public Service Corporation
letters.desc: WEC insists cost allocation rules must prevent cross-subsidies from existing customers to large loads. They support the gross-load default for cost assignment and warn that net-based approaches create shifting risks unless strict controls on actual grid use are in place.
quotes: The WEC Companies are concerned that the process established by any rulemaking will not adequately insulate other customers, resulting in cross-subsidies from Wisconsin Electric's base customers to large load customers.

the Commission should make the "gross" amount of load the default approach for studying large load interconnections consistent with existing Commission precedent.  This will ensure that co-located arrangements are appropriately studied based on their actual use of the transmission system, even if the load or generation has its withdrawal or injection rights based on the net capacity behind the meter.

If the net withdrawal or injection of co-located facilities are permitted to influence transmission cost allocation, the Commission should ensure that there are adequate restrictions on the ability of the load or generation facility to withdraw or inject beyond their respective entitlements.

letters.desc: The Alliance argues that transmission providers must not pass the costs of large-load integration onto existing customers in Tribal or disadvantaged communities. Uniform deposit rules and new queue mechanisms that privilege better-capitalized applicants perpetuate systemic inequities.
quotes: If left unmodified, the ANOPR's proposal to apply uniform study deposit and penalty requirements to large-load interconnections would perpetuate systemic inequities and further restrict Tribal participation in the energy transition.

The Commission should make clear that transmission providers may not shift operational risks, reliability degradation, or the costs of new load integration onto existing customers - particularly those in Tribal and disadvantaged communities.

letters.desc: ATC opposes the ANOPR's 100% direct assignment proposal as overly complex and prone to disputes. It favors continued rolled-in allocation to all benefiting customers, accepts direct assignment only for facilities exclusively used by the new load, and insists that transmission owners retain a reasonable return on investment under any cost framework.
quotes: Limiting applicability to the subset of loads that do not meet with certain operating criteria could provide adequate controls, ensure reliability, contain costs, while preserving the flexibility for transmission owners such as ATC to continue to interconnect traditional, conforming loads based upon our existing interconnection processes.

ATC, along with several stakeholders, supports continued allocation of network upgrade costs to all transmission customers that benefit from the enhanced transmission system, consistent with Commission precedent.
ATC believes such direct assignment would be highly complex and likely result in disputes, confusion, and delays.
Direct assignment should be narrowly tailored to facilities exclusively attributable to and used by new loads to help contain costs and maintain alignment with cost-causation principles.
any future guidance, policy statement, or rulemaking should preserve transmission owners' ability to earn a reasonable return on transmission system investments, consistent with judicial precedent.

Transmission owners must continue to be compensated for the risks associated with owning, operating, and maintaining network upgrades through mechanisms such as initial funding under any future cost-assignment framework.

letters.org: Americans for a Clean Energy Grid
letters.desc: ACEG opposes a strict 100% direct-assignment funding model for load interconnection network upgrades, arguing it would replicate the bottleneck that plagued generator interconnection. The filing supports broad cost allocation across all beneficiaries of the integrated transmission system, consistent with Order 1920 principles, and warns that participant-only funding creates holdout incentives that deter investment. Large loads should pay their proportionate share as part of a multi-value plan, not bear the full cost of upgrades that benefit the wider grid.
quotes: the ANOPR has a significant gap that may jeopardize the ability to achieve the stated goals, by not also specifically tackling the obstacles to building out the transmission needed to interconnect those loads.
for every year of delay of well-planned transmission, there is a 15-35% cost in postponed reliability improvements, reduced access to lower-cost generation, and foregone economic efficiencies.

Building transmission upgrades on a sporadic, piecemeal basis to integrate certain resources is simply less efficient and more expensive than integrating both generation and load through proactive and comprehensive planning.
generation interconnection requests often withdraw from the interconnection queue after studies are completed and the required network upgrades are not constructed.

The Commission has acknowledged that reliance on participant funding as a regional cost allocation method 'increases the incentive of any individual beneficiary to defer investment in the hopes that other beneficiaries will value a transmission project enough to fund its development.'

Large loads that are incorporated into forecasts used to plan and develop new infrastructure should pay their fair share over the life of the asset; planning processes should ensure that such forecasts only incorporate loads that are not speculative or temporary.

Should the Commission revert to a strict direct-assignment funding mechanism for load interconnection-related network upgrades, it risks stymying the very development it seeks to accelerate, as this will only harm transmission developers' ability to attract capital and make needed investments that benefit all transmission users.

As the Commission seeks to accelerate interconnection of new loads, it should do so in conjunction with rapid implementation of Order No. 1920 and require regions to more quickly plan multi-value transmission lines and allocate costs to all customers who use—and benefit from—the integrated transmission system.

letters.desc: Duke Energy argues network upgrades provide system-wide benefits and should receive rolled-in rate treatment consistent with longstanding FERC policy. It recommends a refund-upon-energization mechanism rather than 100 percent direct cost assignment.
quotes: Duke Energy encourages the Commission to re-consider this direct assignment principle and retain its repeatedly and consistently affirmed position that network upgrades are integrated transmission that provide benefits on a system-wide basis, which justifies rolled-in rate treatment.

Duke Energy recommends the adoption of large load interconnection pricing rules that would require large load customers to initially fund the network upgrade (unless the transmission provider elects to initially fund the upgrade), then require the transmission provider to credit or refund back to the large load customer the total amount paid for the required network upgrades.

letters.desc: EPSA opposes using resource adequacy as a basis for determining interconnection cost, arguing it would be discriminatory under open access principles.
quotes: To introduce resource adequacy as a consideration in determining whether and at what cost to interconnect new large load would necessarily discriminate against that new load and existing generators.

letters.desc: Emerald AI opposes requirements to build matching generation, arguing software-defined flexibility is more cost-effective, can be deployed immediately, and achieves the same grid balancing outcome without capital-intensive multi-year buildouts.
quotes: harness the full suite of flexibility technologies in a technology-neutral and performance-based way.
Requiring physical generation (as suggested by the PJM IMM, Monitoring Analytics) erodes the value of software-defined curtailment and unnecessarily increases costs.

If a facility can verifiably reduce its net load at the Point of Interconnection (POI) within a specified timeframe, the method used to achieve that reduction should be irrelevant to the transmission provider.
Building new generation is capital-intensive and delay projects by several years. Software-defined flexibility can be deployed immediately.
Mandating that data centers build matching generation to receive expedited interconnection is economically inefficient and technologically regressive.

letters.desc: Exelon opposes requiring large loads to pay 100% of transmission upgrade costs up front. It argues this approach invokes the 'and' pricing prohibition, letting large loads escape ongoing NITS charges, and ultimately shifts more cost onto other customers than rolled-in allocation would. TSAs are presented as a superior alternative that keeps large loads in the general rate base.
quotes: Large load interconnection frameworks must not only aim to expediently, fairly, and reliably interconnect new customers, these processes must also take care not to exacerbate affordability challenges facing the country.

Overstated demand expectations can, and likely will, trigger costly system upgrades or new facility construction to serve that anticipated demand. If expected demand never materializes, infrastructure and capacity costs can end up borne by other customers.
These agreements are designed to ensure that a contribution to the transmission revenue requirement is made by large load customers commensurate with their requested end-use retail demand.
The design of the TSA is intended to weed out speculative customer behavior while protecting other customers in the event a large load project realizes less than its promised load.

while there is surface appeal to proposals to directly allocate 100 percent of transmission upgrades driven by new large load customers, such an approach may not achieve the goal of avoiding undue cost shifts and may put other customers at considerable risk.

If new large loads are made to be responsible for the costs of upgrades as a requirement to interconnect, pursuant to the Commission's prohibition on 'and' pricing and concerns over undue discrimination, those same loads will undoubtedly maintain that they are not required to pay separately for transmission service (i.e., for network integration transmission service, the 'NITS' rate).

By spreading the revenue requirement for the transmission system generally over an increasing number of billing units--a.k.a. 'increasing the denominator'--it reduces what other customers pay for transmission.
The more large loads are carved out to pay separately for certain transmission infrastructure, the less they will pay for the overall grid and the more other customers will pay.

Exelon does not believe that established principles of rolled-in cost allocation need to be challenged to achieve the aims of the ANOPR and, indeed, an approach that avoids doing so will be both most effective and most expeditious.

such an approach creates challenging dynamics like those we have seen in the generator interconnection space. For example, this approach likely benefits earlier loads that identify favorable interconnection points, only for later large load customers to trigger significant upgrades

letters.desc: The IEA opposes assigning cost recovery for upgrades serving retail load growth under federal tariffs, arguing it would conflict with state ratemaking authority. Cost-allocation rules must be limited to transmission-level network upgrades associated with wholesale transactions, leaving retail cost recovery within state jurisdiction.
quotes: Cost recovery for upgrades that serve retail load growth should remain within state regulators' ratemaking authority. Assigning such costs under federal tariffs could lead to jurisdictional conflicts and undermine established retail cost recovery mechanisms. FERC should clarify that cost-allocation rules developed in this proceeding will apply only to transmission-level network upgrades (as defined by FERC's Seven-Factor Test) associated with wholesale, not retail, transactions.

letters.desc: The filer opposes 100% participant funding as grounded in flawed embedded-cost methodology that ignores marginal impacts. She advocates Ramsey-Boiteux cost allocation, warning that full cost assignment to elastic large loads will push them toward grid defection.
quotes: Current interconnection rules treat these loads as static and inflexible, ignoring capabilities that could significantly reduce system stress and upgrade costs.
Legacy interconnection rules create high asset specificity and hold-up risks, driving developers toward inefficient bypass strategies.
The ANOPR's suggestion of 100% participant funding for upgrades relies on flawed embedded-cost methodologies that ignore marginal impacts.
Efficient cost recovery should instead follow Ramsey-Boiteux principles, allocating fixed costs inversely to elasticity.
Because large loads are highly elastic and can relocate or self-supply, assigning them full upgrade costs encourages inefficient grid defection.

The Commission should establish a federal framework that lowers barriers to flexible resources, modernizes market participation rules for technologies like thermal energy storage (TES), and reforms cost allocation to reflect marginal impacts.

letters.desc: Kiesling opposes both embedded-cost and fully distributed cost methodologies and the ANOPR's 100% participant funding proposal. She argues these methods are economically unsound because they ignore marginal impacts, produce arbitrary results based on queue position, and push elastic large loads toward grid defection. She recommends replacing them with Ramsey-Boiteux inverse-elasticity pricing.
quotes: Current interconnection rules treat these loads as static and inflexible, ignoring capabilities that could significantly reduce system stress and upgrade costs.
The ANOPR's suggestion of 100% participant funding for upgrades relies on flawed embedded-cost methodologies that ignore marginal impacts.
Efficient cost recovery should instead follow Ramsey-Boiteux principles, allocating fixed costs inversely to elasticity.
Because large loads are highly elastic and can relocate or self-supply, assigning them full upgrade costs encourages inefficient grid defection.

Transmission upgrade cost assignment remains one of the least transparent components of the interconnection process. Because most jurisdictions rely on embedded-cost or FDC methods, the relationship between a project's marginal impact and its assigned upgrade cost is weak.
FERC should not adopt a blanket rule obligating large loads to bear 100 percent of assigned upgrade costs without first reforming the allocation methodology to reflect marginal cost principles.
Aligning cost allocation with marginal impacts ensures that flexible loads remain part of the bulk system rather than retreating into private microgrids.

letters.desc: LPPC opposes FERC interference in the terms, conditions, and cost allocation for generation serving large loads. The council argues that assessment and allocation of generation costs for large load service should remain under state authority, not subject to federal mandate.
quotes: LPPC expressed support for the objective articulated by the Department of Energy ("DOE") of a consistent, nationwide approach to large load interconnection. However, LPPC asked that this be accomplished while respecting the role reserved under the Federal Power Act ("FPA") to state authorities over retail service, of which large load is an increasing component.

In its comments, LPPC urged the Commission, should it adopt a rule in this docket, to eschew any intention to interfere with the terms and conditions of retail service, including contractual terms and the assessment and allocation of the cost of generation needed to serve large loads.

letters.desc: FERC must maintain comprehensive visibility over all mechanisms that shift costs to existing consumers, including generator retirements induced by large load service. Reliability studies alone are insufficient to protect consumers from these financial impacts; targeted cost-mitigation policies are required.
quotes: FERC should consider alternative mechanisms to ensure it retains visibility over the full spectrum of actions that have the effect of raising consumer costs and ensure it adopts policies to mitigate such actions.

the reliability studies required by Principle #10 are insufficient to protect consumers from the financial impacts of existing generators retiring from the market to instead serve more lucrative large load customers.

letters.org: Louisiana Public Service CommissionMississippi Public Service Commission
letters.desc: The filing flags cost allocation as a core concern, warning that federal rules could impose undue costs on retail consumers and undermine state mechanisms that fairly distribute infrastructure costs.
quotes: the proposed implementation of that goal raises jurisdictional, reliability, resource adequacy, transparency, planning, and cost allocation concerns

the states have the authority and duty to develop protective measures in approving facilities needed to serve large loads, including measures designed to fairly allocate the costs and to protect reliability so that retail ratepayers are not unfairly burdened

letters.desc: Maven argues LCEP's cost allocation is unanswered: Constellation's filing does not identify who pays for protection systems, remedial action schemes, studies, operator training, harmonics mitigation, or the many other costs that LCEP-enabled service would generate. Any unassigned cost falls on captive ratepayers who did not choose to host data centers. Maven also flags that LCEP's dependence on the host generator's continued operation exposes communities to stranded-cost risk at generator retirement.
quotes: The filing does not demonstrate who pays for the protection systems, remedial action schemes, telemetry, metering, dynamic fault recorders, communications, operator training, reserve requirements, voltage and reactive support, harmonics mitigation, restoration support, affected-system studies, network upgrades discovered through dynamic analysis, enforcement administration, or system impacts from protection misoperation.

Every unaccounted cost that LCEP fails to assign to the applicant is a cost that falls on the ratepayer. The Commission should not adopt a replacement rate that treats cost allocation as an afterthought.

A service that disappears when the host generator retires is not infrastructure. It is a monetization strategy for a depreciating asset—and the stranded-cost risk, when that asset retires, falls on the communities and ratepayers left behind.

letters.desc: Maven Solutions opposes FirstEnergy's expansion-rate proposal as a misapplication of cost-causation doctrine. The filing argues that triggering a transmission upgrade does not equal bearing its full cost; proper allocation requires a benefit study that accounts for regional reliability, congestion relief, and future load service. The proposal also secures transmission-owner revenue while shifting all risk to the customer, and its reallocation mechanism is unspecified.
quotes: The natural-gas analogy is directionally useful and structurally false.

Electric transmission is a meshed alternating-current network in which power flows simultaneously over all transmission paths according to electrical characteristics—not according to contractual designations.

A transmission facility built to interconnect a data center may simultaneously improve regional reliability, reduce congestion, increase transfer capability, support future load service, and enable generation deliverability for parties who had no part in the interconnection request.
The proposal does not eliminate the bottleneck. It monetizes it.

FirstEnergy's framework guarantees the transmission owner's cost recovery, collateralizes the transmission owner's investment, and shifts all demand-forecast, utilization, and cancellation risk from the utility to the customer.
"Triggered by a data center" is not the same as "benefits only a data center." FirstEnergy wants the causation label without doing the beneficiary math.
The Commission cannot approve a framework that announces reallocation as a concept without specifying it as a mechanism.

Political pledges and filed-rate obligations are different instruments. The Commission should not confuse a White House press event with the evidentiary record required to support a just-and-reasonable rate under FPA §§ 205–206.
FirstEnergy's expansion-rate proposal is, in part, a direct response to that litigation. The filing says: do not block the project—fix the rate design.
A rate-design framework that assigns capital costs without addressing dynamic-load performance creates a dangerous half-solution.

Collateral requirements must be proportional to risk, not designed to exclude smaller competitors. A framework that only trillion-dollar hyperscalers can satisfy entrenches the largest firms while pricing out smaller developers, manufacturers, and emerging industries.
The gas analogy is useful as a directional signal. It is false as a one-to-one regulatory mapping.

letters.desc: MISO opposes requiring 100% direct cost assignment to large load customers, arguing this reduces the creative cost-recovery arrangements between load-serving entities and large loads that currently help bring projects online. MISO also notes that the generator queue's speculative-withdrawal problem would carry cost implications into any load queue.
quotes: utilizing a generator interconnection process as a template that historically has experienced delays and is unlikely to provide the speed to power needed by large load customers

only about 13% of the total capacity entering interconnection queues nationwide ultimately achieves commercial operation.  Withdrawals of speculative interconnection requests frequently require restudies, particularly for later-stage withdrawals, which in turn could delay completion of studies and ultimately delay bringing viable generation proposals online.

This principle would call for MISO allocating such costs directly to the large load customer.  MISO has concerns with this approach as it may reduce the options and flexibility that exist today between the LSE, large load customer, and possibly the retail jurisdiction, to develop creative approaches for cost recovery to more readily facilitate siting of new large load additions.

letters.desc: The filer opposes both direct assignment of upgrade costs to load and any option-to-build right for large load owners, viewing both as departures from proven MISO tariff practices. They argue the Eleventh and Twelfth Principles would create cost-allocation distortions and undue discrimination.
quotes: requiring direct assignment of upgrade costs to interconnecting load would mark a fundamental shift when there is no clear basis or purpose for doing so.

Under long-standing Commission precedent, the costs of network upgrades required to interconnect load are allocated to transmission customers through transmission rates under Schedule 9 of the MISO Tariff.  LSEs, in turn, pass on those costs to their retail customers.
the MISO Transmission Owners oppose extending the option to build to large load owners
the MISO Transmission Owners are concerned that the Eleventh and Twelfth Principles raise significant cost allocation concerns, as well as undue discrimination concerns

letters.desc: The filer opposes ANOPR proposals to shift network upgrade costs to large load owners through direct assignment or to alter ancillary service billing, arguing these changes violate cost causation principles and will create litigation.
