quotes: the MISO Transmission Owners urge the Commission to maintain its long-standing policy in favor of rolled-in rate treatment for network upgrades triggered by load additions, including large load additions, as opposed to requiring direct assignment of network upgrades associated with large load interconnections

network upgrades by definition benefit all transmission customers, so it is consistent with cost causation principles that all transmission customers, including large load owners, be allocated costs payable through transmission rates when they take transmission service

Maintaining the status quo of cost responsibility for transmission service and ancillary services will provide large load owners and transmission providers clarity and certainty and avoid preventable and unnecessary litigation.

Basing load owners' transmission service responsibilities on their withdrawal rights alone fails to account for transmission service large load owners will use during the planned and unplanned outages that generators experience, i.e., times when large load owners will benefit from the broader transmission system.

letters.desc: The filing quantifies cost shifts to existing PJM customers from adding data center load without new generation, estimating up to $5.48 billion per year in capacity market costs alone. It opposes co-location, connect-and-manage, and demand-side substitutes as mechanisms that defer or spread these costs to others. All customers must pay full NITS costs.
quotes: Commenters with specific proposals generally seek to avoid the only just, reasonable and not unduly discriminatory action available to the Commission that will protect reliability and affordability for existing customers which is to provide clear incentives to large new data center loads to get to market quickly and reliably and to refuse to permit reliability to be undermined by adding large new data center loads without corresponding new generation.
State regulators cannot protect retail customers from the impact of adding large new data center loads on PJM wholesale market prices for capacity, energy and reserves and on system reliability.

Co-located load is simply a way to wish away the reliability issue and more importantly to undermine the PJM markets and impose unacceptably large reliability and monetary costs on all other PJM customers.

If 20,000 MW of new data center load were added and 90 percent or less of this load were offered in the capacity market as emergency demand side resources, the Market Monitor estimates that the increased cost of capacity would be around $5.48 billion per year to existing customers.

The narrowly defined co-location model that is the subject of Constellation's Complaint and Constellation's ongoing comments in the PJM CIFP process would allow existing generation to sell to a large new data center load and withdraw from the PJM capacity market. If allowed, this option could lead to the end of PJM markets.

The Market Monitor agrees with PJM's points and thinks that PJM understates the negative outcomes of connect and manage. Ignoring the issues at the time of interconnection and imposing the actual costs as they are realized on other customers is not consistent with the stated purpose of the ANOPR.

All customers should be full NITS customers and pay their full share of transmission costs without calculations of asserted gross impacts, net impacts or other attempts to avoid paying for transmission service.

letters.desc: NCAI opposes the compressed comment period of 24 total days as procedurally insufficient for Tribal governments to conduct internal review, legal analysis, and leadership deliberation required before submitting an official position. The minimal 7-day extension fails to accommodate sovereign governmental processes that are mandated by federal law and the spirit of the APA.
quotes: the minimal 7-day extension — granted only in response to state organizations citing "technical and legal complexity" — remains profoundly insufficient
Tribal governments must conduct internal governmental review, legal analysis, and leadership deliberation before submitting an official position
Compressing this process into a total of 24 days renders meaningful participation effectively impossible and violates the spirit of the Administrative Procedure Act

letters.desc: Local electric consumers should not be required to subsidize network upgrades and interconnection costs of new large loads. State regulators must ensure that costs directly associated with local transmission upgrades are paid by the entity installing the large load.
quotes: Local electric consumers should not be required to subsidize the network upgrades and interconnection costs of new large loads.

letters.org: New England States Committee on Electricity
letters.desc: At least 20 states already have large load tariffs that address reliability and cost allocation, including financial commitments and curtailment protocols. The ANOPR as proposed would create confusion about these programs, potentially strand costs for existing customers, and disrupt projects already underway.
quotes: at least 20 states have approved or have pending large load tariffs or similar measures, which may include financial commitments, curtailment protocols, and minimum contract terms to allow for the rapid interconnection of large loads without compromising grid reliability or unduly burdening existing retail customers

The ANOPR, as proposed, would create confusion as to the effect of these efforts and could compromise reliability, disrupt existing projects, create stranded costs for customers, and invite otherwise unnecessary legal challenges.

letters.desc: NDPSC is concerned that reclassifying large loads outside retail tariffs would prevent cost-spreading benefits for existing retail customers, shifting burdens to them.
quotes: Most concerning to the NDPSC is the potential for unintended negative impacts to the ratepayers in our state. The language of the ANOPR presents a scenario where existing customers would not be able to benefit from spreading a utility's generation and distribution fixed costs over additional energy sales if large loads are not subject to a utility's retail tariff provisions.

letters.desc: OPSI argues that cost responsibility and cost causation analysis for large load interconnections is a retail ratemaking function within state jurisdiction. FERC rules must not block state prudency reviews or shift costs to ratepayers who did not cause them.
quotes: FERC should "preserve and affirm states' retail regulatory authority under the FPA, ensure that large load interconnections do not compromise grid reliability or impose undue costs on retail customers, and respect state tools for promoting system flexibility and equitable cost allocation."
It is imperative that large loads looking to interconnect bear their fair share of transmission costs and that the Commission deter harmful speculation as these loads seek to interconnect.

FERC rules must not impede the state's traditional right to perform prudency reviews and conduct cost causation analysis necessary to protect local ratepayers from costs they did not cause, especially where transmission charges are based on withdrawal rights.

letters.desc: PG&E opposes a uniform 100% cost assignment rule and advocates for refund mechanisms tied to retail revenues, cost containment for customer-built facilities, and state-specific cost frameworks.
quotes: PG&E believes that three key principles are essential to any final Commission rule: Protecting existing ratepayers from incurring additional or stranded costs while also adopting fair and equitable cost responsibility and allocation approaches for large load customers; Appropriately balancing state and Commission jurisdiction and developing a complimentary and cooperative framework, while also ensuring timely state action on large load issues; and Developing clear rules that will expedite large load interconnections by allowing flexibility rather than imposing additional requirements that slow the interconnection process.
Third, requiring a large load or hybrid facility to pay 100% of the network upgrade costs without any opportunity for refunds is contrary to judicial and Commission precedent.

Large load and hybrid customers should be eligible for refunds based on the electric retail revenues produced from these facilities. Unlike generators, which often do not pay retail electric rates and do not produce substantial revenues which can offset interconnection infrastructure costs, large load and hybrid facilities generally pay retail electric rates which, in part, offset the costs of the infrastructure needed for these facilities.

The Commission should avoid a one-size-fits-all approach to cost responsibility and refunds especially given the unique rate structures and designs in each state. Instead, the Commission should allow utilities and/or states to develop a cost responsibility and refund proposal that is right for that utility and/or state.
the Commission should include in its final rule cost containment provisions for customer built facilities to avoid the construction of facilities that are excessively expensive.

letters.desc: The PA PUC argues that FERC-mandated interconnections and network upgrades may unfairly burden retail ratepayers if not properly allocated, and that states are better positioned to determine reasonable rate structures for large load customers.
quotes: The recommendations that (1) load and hybrid facilities be studied together with generating facilities for efficient siting and be subject to standardized study deposits, readiness requirements, and withdrawal penalties; (2) hybrid facilities be studied based on the amount of injection and/or withdrawal rights requested to provide incentives for co-location with new generation facilities; (3) any hybrid interconnection install the system protection facilities necessary to prevent unauthorized injections or withdrawals that exceed the respective rights; (4) financial penalties for load facilities and hybrid facilities; (5) expedited consideration of interconnection studies of large loads and hybrid facilities that agree to be curtailable and dispatchable; and (6) that load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades that are assigned through the interconnection studies all have widespread economic and political ramifications.

The PA PUC submits that states are in the best position as electric retail service regulators to determine the reasonableness of electric retail rate structures regarding the distribution of service, including service to customers with peak loads over 20 MW.

letters.desc: PPL argues that existing utility ratemaking, combined with load guarantee agreements requiring data centers to purchase at least 80% of contracted load over five years, already protects network customers without the deterrent effect of 100% upfront network upgrade cost assignment.
quotes: The ANOPR proposes that under federal interconnection rules, 'load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of the network upgrades that they are assigned through interconnection studies.' Should the Commission adopt the ANOPR and assume control over large load interconnection, it should interpret this language consistent with its longstanding policy that network customers pay for network upgrades.

Charging large retail loads 100% of the network upgrade costs required to interconnect them to the transmission system would dramatically increase the Day 1 costs of data center interconnections. This will inevitably lead to slower process, higher costs, and fewer data centers being constructed.

PPL Electric requires interconnecting large load customers like data centers to enter into ESAs with provisions guaranteeing they will purchase at least 80% of the aggregate load requested over an initial term of five years. This electric service commitment ensures that the new load pays aggregate transmission service charges that are at least equal to the total expenses incurred by PPL Electric for construction work included in the rate base.
Unlike upfront payment by large loads, this process does not disincentivize new load connections and does not violate longstanding ratemaking principles.

letters.desc: Allowing direct transmission connection enables wheeling arrangements that could expose existing customers to higher LMP pricing from congestion, force costly transmission additions that recover through zone-wide rates, create resource adequacy gaps, and deny legacy customers the benefits of large load cost-sharing.
quotes: An unintended consequence of allowing large load customers to connect directly to the transmission system could be that the customer is able to generate its own power offsite and wheel the power through the transmission system to serve itself. This type of arrangement could lead to unintended consequences such as: 1) exposing existing customers to higher LMP pricing due to congestion, 2) causing the local transmission owner to build additional transmission to address reliability issues created by the large load (which costs would then be assigned to the local zone and recovered from all customers in the zone), 3) lead to resource adequacy challenges, and 4) will deprive other customers of benefits of the large load.

Like our federal counterparts, we strive for the development of a safe, reliable, and efficient system, while safeguarding customers from increasing costs. We advocate for a system that is orderly constructed, non-discriminatory, and that allows our vertically-integrated incumbent utilities to continue to provide retail service to customers pursuant to their state-mandated service obligations.

letters.desc: SMA contends that full network upgrade cost assignment would raise the cost of new domestic steel investments and conflict with federal policy supporting domestic steel production against global dumping.
quotes: The SMA is concerned that FERC's NOPR would require new load customers to shoulder 100 percent of all network upgrade costs identified in the interconnection study.
While data centers may be able to absorb these costs without rendering their projects uneconomic, new electric arc furnace steel mills almost certainly cannot.

Imposing these costs on steelmakers would undermine the administration's strong policy commitment to expanding domestic steel production, potentially making new steel investments more costly and increasing costs for American steelmakers battling steel being dumped globally.

letters.desc: Senators oppose spreading data center transmission costs to residential ratepayers and urge FERC to reject filings that do not properly allocate costs. They cite PJM's tripled capacity auction costs and call for proactive investigation into discriminatory utility practices.
quotes: PJM's 2024 capacity market auction, which aims to secure resources to guarantee that the grid will be able to meet peak demand in the coming months, closed at a record high of $16.6 billion, up from just $2.2 billion in 2023.

In order to protect ratepayers from unreasonable or unjust price hikes driven by data center energy demand, FERC should reject transmission-related filings that do not properly address cost allocation or allow the cost of transmission built to serve data centers to be spread across the region.

Beyond addressing proposals as they are presented to FERC, the Commission must proactively investigate and act if it finds the practices of a regional operator or utility to be unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory, or preferential to data centers at the expense of residential ratepayers.

As FERC considers Energy Secretary Chris Wright's recent request for a rulemaking to standardize and accelerate the interconnection of large loads like data centers, We urge FERC to prioritize the concerns of residential ratepayers.

letters.desc: Large load projects require transmission and distribution upgrades, and state commissions hold authority over retail cost recovery. The UTC is concerned that a federal process focused on transmission access could enable cross-subsidy and undermine the UTC's role in ensuring just and reasonable retail rates.
quotes: establishing a standardized, national process for large load interconnection may provide benefits for Washington utility customers. Any benefits of a standardized process must be weighed against the significant risks that blurring the jurisdictional boundaries of regulation could compromise Washington State's own energy policy goals, negatively impact affordability, compromise reliability, and miss opportunities for states to develop new solutions to large load interconnection issues.

Large loads often require upgrades to both the transmission and distribution system and utilities must demonstrate that new load will not be served by imposing undue costs on existing customers. Cost recovery is ultimately approved by the UTC, which is responsible for ensuring retail rates are just, reasonable, and non-discriminatory.

A federal interconnection process focused on transmission access may not maintain the essential role that the UTC (and other state commissions) play in ensuring fair retail electric rates that are free from cross subsidy.

letters.desc: Large loads directly impact infrastructure adequacy and wholesale rates, with data center load growth now driving 63 percent of PJM capacity price increases. FERC's mandate includes protecting customers from excessive prices, making this a core regulatory concern.
quotes: FERC's jurisdiction over wholesale rates includes the responsibility to ensure customers are "protect[ed] 'against excessive prices' and [to] ensure effective transmission of electric power."

the new large loads present important economic and technological opportunities for our nation; however, due to their unprecedented size, these loads are having, and will continue to have, a direct impact on resource and infrastructure adequacy across the nation which have corresponding impacts on wholesale rates
63% of the increase in capacity prices in the 2025/26 auction can be attributed to data centers, translating to $9.3 billion in infrastructure costs that will be passed on to ratepayers

letters.desc: ECA argues that new large loads need not raise rates for existing customers but the outcome depends entirely on transmission planning and cost allocation choices. No single allocation method resolves all concerns: targeted direct assignment aligns better with cost causation but creates disputes and risks foregoing rate-spreading benefits, while broader regional approaches risk misaligning costs with causal loads. The timing of when costs enter rates can matter as much as the ultimate allocation.
quotes: the timing of cost recovery can be as important as the ultimate allocation of costs. Transmission costs may enter rates before anticipated load growth fully materializes, creating a risk that existing customers temporarily or permanently bear costs incurred to serve future demand.

no single transmission cost allocation methodology is likely to address all stakeholder concerns. More targeted approaches may better align with cost-causation principles but may also generate disputes regarding attribution of transmission needs and costs.

Adding new electricity demand to the system need not raise rates for existing customers—and in fact can put downward pressure on existing customer rates—but that depends on the policy choices federal and state regulators make now.

The most durable path is likely to combine strong state retail tariffs, better and more granular federal-state alignment, improved transparency, targeted federal reforms where transmission costs, planning processes, or cost allocation decisions are beyond the reach of state retail regulation, alongside innovative new customer-centric approaches to transmission planning and expansion outside traditional approaches.

singling out large load-driven regional transmission costs may appear to improve alignment with the cost causation principle in the near term, but could undermine more efficient, multi-value regional planning that produces broader long-term benefits for consumers.

letters.desc: The brief notes through a Wyoming PSC official's statement that cost causation allocation is practically difficult, illustrating why the federal rulemaking must grapple with cost questions that state regulators are already finding complex.
quotes: ensuring costs are allocated to the party that causes them is 'a super complicated, involved affair when you're actually doing it.'

letters.org: New York State Public Service Commission
letters.desc: Large loads create generation needs and other system costs that extend beyond the interconnection itself and are ultimately borne by all customers. The NYSPSC asserts that state regulators, with oversight of T&D utilities, are best positioned to identify and allocate those costs fairly.
quotes: current interconnection processes in New York require large loads to pay for the cost of their interconnection and related transmission upgrades, the operation of large loads may impose other costs not reflected in the interconnection process.

these large loads will require significant amounts of generation and their appearance on the electric grid will add to the need for more generation to meet statewide electric demand needs and thereby raise the costs for all customers.
Given the NYPSC's regulatory oversight of the T&D utilities, the NYPSC is in the best position to identify these costs and allocate them appropriately.

letters.desc: PJM highlights that cost allocation rules for study deposits, withdrawal penalties, and upgrade costs associated with a new federal load queue remain undefined and would require significant tariff development.
quotes: While the prospect of a federally-regulated large load interconnection process warrants further exploration, PJM encourages FERC to seize available opportunities to issue nearer-term regulatory guidance on matters squarely within its wholesale and transmission jurisdiction about:  resource adequacy, the provision of ancillary services, mandatory operational regimes, potential wholesale rate classes for different types of load customers, interconnection and transmission planning, cost allocation, and NERC and Tariff reliability obligations and requirements.

questions would need to be answered about whether such a new process will necessarily lead to different or enhanced large load interconnection results, and whether the theoretical benefits of a federally-regulated large load interconnection process outweigh the challenges of creating and administering a load queue at the RTO/ISO level.

what are just and reasonable rates for any standardized study deposits, readiness requirements, and withdrawal penalties?  Would the federal load interconnection process and rate levels look to state law analogues where such constructs have already been developed?  Will such rates be postage stamp rates or connected to the scope and scale of the proposed load interconnection?
